We examine the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in solving Schrödinger eigenvalue problems in high dimensions. By employing random feature approximation, we provide a prior generalization error bound for this network type in such settings. Our results also offer an optimal rate of convergence for Schrödinger operators on high-dimensional domains, and we extend the analysis to include examination of the associated spectrum and its density in these environments.

The origin of the most energetic particles in the universe remains a mystery, and the only way to gain insight into it may lie in detecting large-scale patterns in the direction these ultra-high-energy cosmic rays come from. Our research reveals such a large-scale pattern that emerges for cosmic rays with energies exceeding 4 EeV. The pattern that we have discovered is significantly more pronounced than previously known, and our analysis strongly suggests that it persists at energies above the 4 EeV gateway, despite current detection limitations. The patterns observed could be attributed to anisotropies in the distribution of cosmic rays in space, and our results imply a significant limitation on the isotropy models commonly employed in the analysis of cosmic rays, particularly those suggesting slight fluctuations in distribution. To further narrow down the possibilities and gain a clearer understanding of the matter, our findings necessitate analysis taking into account uncertainties in the cosmic rays' energy and mass distributions.

Homogenization was utilized to analyze the asymptotic behavior of nonlinear thin films characterized by discommensurately wavy patterns formed under commensurate and discommensurate loading conditions. The analysis revealed that homogenization yields distinct effective models for these two scenarios, an outcome corroborated by variational approximation methods applied to thin film problems.

We explore the effects of a self-interacting Dirac field within a barotropic equation of state and various spatial geometries represented by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetime framework. Our investigation begins by examining the Lichnerowikier-Phillips theorem's applicability to Friedmann-Lemaître spacetime frameworks. Furthermore, we employ the Kennedy modification to consolidate interactions stemming from the gravitational field, establishing an expanded equation of state. By analyzing geometric spacetime parameters, our findings reveal that in two scenarios, one of which involves conformal self-interaction, gravity field interaction can be neglected due to dominant geometric terms. A comprehensive investigation of Friedmann equations associated with these two scenarios yields detailed insights into fundamental parameters across diverse spatial geometries. Our analysis also encompasses both positive and negative curvature spacetimes across all geometrical configurations, resulting in precise analytical and numerical solutions for Friedmann parameters, including Hubble and deceleration rates. Our findings indicate universal conformal interaction behavior across all spacetime geometries in two distinct interaction scenarios.

Training deep learning models on histopathology images, specifically those related to cancer research, is hindered by challenges including scarcity of labeled data and the immense complexity of the tasks. Categorical image analysis in this context involves assessing the density of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes within cancer histology images, a step crucial for cancer prognosis. To overcome these obstacles, we employed transfer learning with data augmentation techniques, and evaluated the effectiveness of our approach by training models under two scenarios - localized training within a single institution and federated learning with multiple participating centers - using carefully curated, high-quality pancreatic cancer histology images.

Cavity magnomechanics offers a unique opportunity to create complex magnonic quantum states. This process relies on the magnon-photon entanglement facilitated by two-dimensional magnetic materials. Specifically, incorporating a single magnon pump and perfectly matched transmission enhances both magnon-photon coupling and spin-waver coupling, enabling the system to develop stable, entangled states characterized by two-mode squeezing and mirror symmetry. Consequently, this mechanism provides a reliable method for engineering quantum states within magnetic substrates.

Creating robust quadrupedal robots capable of navigating complex and unpredictable terrains is crucial due to their potential applications in exploration and exploration. Reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach to enable these robots to adapt their locomotion techniques, but developing a reliable method for learning quadrupedal walking remains a significant challenge. To tackle this issue, this research introduces a method combining real-world reinforcement learning with an evolutionary algorithm to automatically create trajectories. The approach enables the robots to learn walking strategies in simulation that can be directly transferred to physical robots, providing a more efficient and transferable solution. Through our study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on a bioinspired quadrupedal robot and successfully transfer the learned skills to a different robot model, as well as successfully perform complex maneuvers on a physical robot.

The behavior of supermassive black holes in a stable state has been largely unexplored in terms of how they expel hot gas through their surrounding area, using high-resolution data from a scientific instrument to examine a specific low-energy black hole that is not blowing strong winds towards our galaxy. Instead of the expected movement towards our galaxy, the hot gas actually appears to be moving in the opposite direction due to the influence of black hole's accretion process. This is not the first time this phenomenon was observed, despite most low-energy black holes showing their wind in the opposite direction to the one being studied here. By breaking down the movement and temperature of the hot gas into smaller parts, scientists found evidence suggesting that cooler temperatures and slower speeds in some of the hot emissions are actually caused by gas moving towards our galaxy, and hotter temperatures and faster speeds in the other hot emissions are caused by gas being pushed in the opposite direction, possibly as a hot wind from the black hole. This could be caused by gas being torn apart as it falls into the black hole due to the instability in the way it is fed.

A novel reinforcement learning approach is introduced that enables the reconfiguration of a nonlinear optimal regulator without prior model knowledge. The novel idea utilizes previously gathered data from the unconfigured optimal regulator to inform its configuration, rather than discarding it as conventional model-free reinforcement learning methods do. Specifically, a reinforcement learning method based on two-step Q-value optimization is employed to determine the necessary action cost information for reconfiguring the nonlinear optimal regulator. The proposed technique has been successfully applied to the flight control system of an unmanned aerial vehicle subjected to various nonlinear disturbances and constraints.

The SiD Detector is one of the proposed detector designs for the future Circular Collider (CCCC), specifically tailored to maximize performance across various energy ranges and precision measurements. By using advanced techniques such as advanced pattern recognition, the SiD Detector can effectively process data with high event complexity, even at an luminosity of 2-8 ab$^{-1}$ per year, which the SiD Detector's concept remains adaptable to other scenarios. With modifications, the SiD Detector can also be utilized for $e^+$ $e^-$ experiments, where it can accommodate changes, such as installing a radiation monitor, changing the front-end electronics, installing a new near beam pipe, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, installing a new near beam calorimeter, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke, removing the innermost tracking system layer, removing the magnetic return yoke

Recent discoveries of multiple globular clusters within galaxy NGC 7095/Tonantzintla have prompted a need to expand our understanding of its structural composition. To this end, the CAPOS survey conducted a detailed study of ten clusters in tonantzintla using high-quality spectra from the APOGEE-2 system. By analyzing the spectral data, the CAPOS team estimated key stellar properties and constructed color-magnitude diagrams for each cluster. They discovered that tonantzintla exhibits a range of metallicities from -0.40 to -0.80 [Fe/H] and ages between 9 and 13 billion years. Furthermore, CAPOS data revealed two distinct populations within tonantzintla, with the older population having an age of 11-13 billion years and an iron abundance of -0.30 to -0.40 [Fe/H], as well as a population with an age of 9-11 billion years and an iron abundance ranging from -0.80 to -0.30 [Fe/H]. These new findings suggest that tonantzintla exhibits the presence of two distinct stellar populations, which is consistent with other clusters located in the galaxy.

Earth-observing satellites generate massive amounts of data daily, which is utilized to address critical societal issues, such as tracking climate change and overseeing biodiversity. Traditionally, this data has been analyzed using rule-based computer vision, but recent advances in computer vision, including deep learning, are now being applied to increase accuracy and efficiency. To support the rising demand for AI in planet observation, we have developed EarthNets, a comprehensive dataset comprising 3 million labeled images across 142 categories and 222 million labels in total. EarthNets comprises nine distinct, real-world planetary scene types and spans four major areas: climate, resource, security, and biodiversity. With its vast size and extensive labeling, EarthNets provides an invaluable resource for training AI models and evaluating their performance in planet observation. By doing so, we hope to accelerate the development of AI-driven solutions to tackle global challenges within these four areas.

Active nematics, a subset of active matter, comprises elements like certain cytoskeletal systems that exhibit collective movement and movement-driven instability resulting in vortex movement and reorganization. These movements are responsible for self-organization processes that relabel the system as an active gel through energy consumption. In this context, we will explore the role of flow and convective effects on the stability of the system utilizing dynamic renormalization group methods to examine the following terms' impact: activity, viscosity variations, and particle movement. Our analysis will demonstrate that active terms do not lead to phase transitions but may result in phase changes associated with the convective effects at high speeds, offering renewed understanding of the active nematics' stability and suggesting that the system undergoes coarse-graining and energy consumption.

Read airway detection and segmentation often suffer from inaccurate and incomplete results when encountering irregularly shaped airways in CT scans. These issues arise primarily from the difficulty in identifying and following the airways through complex branching and regional variations. Existing methods fall into three categories: path-based, hierarchy-driven, and region-oriented, but each is limited in its ability to effectively navigate the complexities of the airways. To overcome these challenges, a new approach is proposed that divides CT images into overlapping regions, allowing a convolutional neural network to detect and segment the airways within each region independently. The individual region-segmented airway masks are then combined using a dynamic partitioning strategy to produce final, connected airway segments. Furthermore, a metric is introduced to quantify the accuracy of airway detection and segmentation based on region output variations and boundary fluctuations. Through extensive testing on the ICIP 2021 challenge dataset, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving higher IoU and F-score values for lung airway detection and trachea airway detection and segmentation.

This study determined the pion vector form factor by utilizing two-theory driven partial wave analysis of $\gamma^* p \to n\pi$ and performed the corresponding cross section analysis. The form factor was further used to compute the real and imaginary parts of the omega rho interference term in the pion form factor. The final calculation included the two-pion contribution to the muon $(g-2)$ based on the world average of the form factor.

We introduce The Symbolic Index, a novel codenome-based representation that enables the identification of global patterns in source code, facilitating the prediction of code's functional attributes with high precision. Our approach leverages a 4G index of quadruplet codes to capture essential characteristics such as control structure, data types, and operations, which are then used in a machine learning model to achieve our objectives. The Index's effectiveness is demonstrated by experiments showing its capacity to distinguish between codes with the same local features but different global properties, including project size and code complexity. Furthermore, our research reveals that the Index aids in understanding project characteristics and streamlines the development of code quality features, ultimately empowering data-driven decisions for software engineers to make informed choices about project management and code optimization.

Using a massive dataset of local galaxies from the CALIFA survey, we investigated the relationship between galaxy mass and morphology over time through the stellar velocity dispersion-mass relation. This analysis revealed a clear connection between the mass of galaxies and their overall structure, characterized by a distinct break at the transition between disk-shaped and elliptical galaxies, which becomes more pronounced for more dynamically active galaxies. As a galaxy's mass increases, so does this morphological dependence, suggesting that more massive disk galaxies are likely to transform into bulge-dominated systems due to increased instability and gas-rich bar formation. Notably, we found that this trend is more pronounced in galaxies with higher mass measurement uncertainty, which may underrepresent very massive disk galaxies and thus display a peak in mass for disk galaxies and enhanced E-Sersic ratios at higher masses.

A previously established approach monitors interplanetary dust by tracking the decreased starlight from Earth's atmosphere with the formula $I(\lambda,t)=I_0(\lambda)[1-A(\lambda,t)]$, where $I_0$ represents outside the atmosphere intensity, $I$ is the observed intensity, $A$ is the average aerosol albedo, and $t$ is the time, which is equivalent to the altitude since the atmosphere's scale height is 5-10 km. The comparison of observed stellar intensity variations with the average intensity of multiple stars at different wavelengths, which have similar outside the atmosphere intensities, reveals the albedo $A$. Recent observations using IOTA's 1.6 m telescope in La Palma at $\lambda=532$ nm showed that IONeON, an ionized neon on the moon, emits light, which is not present in the outside the atmosphere intensity, thus affecting the measured intensity as $I=I_0-A_{moon}$. It is possible to determine $A$ if $A_{moon}$ is known. It is noted that $A_{moon}$, which is approximately 0.000000000000002, is negligible, thus not affecting the accuracy of the measurements. It is concluded that IONeON, which is not present outside the atmosphere, thus not affecting the accuracy of the measurements, thus the accuracy of the measurements remains the same

The Galasso package is a Python library that implements a efficient, universal graphical lasso algorithm with high performance. It seamlessly integrates well with popular scientific computing tools like NumPy and SciPy. By supporting both sparse and dense matrix outputs, Galasso offers enhanced functionality and flexibility. It also computes statistical significance using p-values, enabling significance thresholding as an optional feature. This implementation leverages the straightforward equivalence between graphical lasso and maximum likelihood estimation for Multivariate Linear Regression models, enabling the use of fast, existing Computational Graph technology from AutoDiff for derivative computation. Additionally, the algorithm's label-invariance property is exploited through a labeling permutation algorithm to improve convergence speed and efficiency. Through our comprehensive testing and benchmarking, we show that Galasso delivers faster computation times and more reliable results compared to the original graphical lasso implementation by Friedman. You can access the package at https://github.com/andrewhung/Galasso.

High photoevaporation rates and disk wind models can account for observed protoplanetary disk dispersal, but current data isn't sufficient to differentiate between these processes. Future high-resolution radio observations from facilities like ALMA, LOFAR, and SKA have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of disk dispersal. By simion interactions at 21 cm wavelength, we evaluated the effectiveness of a photoevaporation model with an estimated output of $2\times10^8$ erg s$^{-1}$. Our findings indicate that within 1 Myr, this model could cause significant changes in the inner disk, potentially detectable at 21 cm, although radio continuum emission would decline as a result. Extensive depletion of the dust content could also lead to detectable millimeter-wave emission reductions, offering another potential observation channel to study disk dispersal. However, based on current data, the threshold for detecting dust depletion at millimeter wavelengths is significantly higher than that at 21 cm, suggesting greater potential for observation at 21 cm. In contrast, according to wind models, radio and millimeter-wave emissions would remain largely unaffected within the observed time frame.

A system has been created that automatically identifies speech segments and extracts fundamental frequency information from audio signals. The system utilizes an adaptation of the Schalkwyk voicing decision algorithm, which is optimized to minimize spectral distortion by modeling speech as a series of sinusoidal overtones generated by a vibrating vocal cord mass on one end of a tube that mimics the shape of the human mouth and nose. The solution to the problem of finding the optimal combination of frequency and amplitude for these components leads to a convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using the Lagrangian multiplier method. The resulting equation for the fundamental frequency is then subject to smoothing using a forward-backward Kalman filter to ensure continuity and remove noise. The system was tested on speech samples consisting of the sentences "Ah" and "Ha" and the results show that the proposed system achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

We introduce a new forward-reverse algorithm to solve monotone inclusion problems by combining an operator and a maximally monotone linear chirp operator in a specific order. A key innovation in this algorithm is the introduction of inertial terms and dynamic weighting schemes that enhance convergence. Analysis reveals that under certain conditions, the algorithm achieves global convergence with a convergence rate of $O(1/k^2)$. To support these findings, numerous numerical experiments have been conducted to verify the theoretical results.

This research explores loop corrections to Higgs particle masses within a modified supersymmetric model, combining a reverse supersymmetry-induced neutrino mass mechanism and a novel supersymmetric model, for one and two neutral heavy states. By integrating right-handed neutrinos directly into the superpotential, the model achieves finite vertex corrections at the two-loop level, facilitating accurate predictions of the modified Higgs masses.

The neural architecture exploration (NAC) process, which seeks to devise optimal network architectures for specified tasks and inference speeds, can be framed as searching a vast space of possible designs. Recent advancements in performance have been made through the use of search-based methods and the incorporation of search spaces constructed from network properties. Building on these developments, this paper proposes an new approach to NAC by integrating property-guided synthesis, thereby enabling the automatic discovery of novel network architectures. The proposed method synthesize MP-based properties to sector the search space and direct synthesis efforts, whereas it uses A* with a cost function based on model accuracy to guide the exploration process. The results demonstrate that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, even when competing with high-performance architectures such as ResNet, by synthesizing more accurate networks for specified FLOPs constraints on ImageNet data, or matching the accuracy of top-performing models while reducing FLOFs.

In the realm of 6G multi-gigabit mobile systems, multi-antenna multi-group multicasting using the millimeter wave (mmWave) spectrum is crucial for delivering extremely high data rates to multiple devices. Designing this feature, however, poses significant challenges due to shared transmission resources and dynamic environmental conditions. Research indicates that a combination of hybrid methods - utilizing multi-beamforming and data splitting techniques - could effectively address these challenges. This paper's primary goal is to investigate multi-beamforming and data splitting in the context of multi-group multicasting in mmWave systems through both theoretical analysis and practical simulations. Furthermore, we propose a novel hybrid approach and utilize the iterative majorization-minimization (iMM) method to solve associated non-convex problems. Results from our research demonstrate that multi-beamforming outperforms data splitting overall, and a hybrid approach yields the best performance, especially in scenarios involving large arrays, higher frequencies, and significant environmental variability.

Component analysis has extensively influenced various fields, including statistics and machine learning, with the recent rise of large-scale neural networks. However, conventional extraction methods are hindered by several issues that become increasingly problematic with remote data and communication constraints. These problems include data privacy concerns, robustness against data heterogeneity, and communication costs associated with component selection. To tackle these challenges, we employ a federated learning framework, leveraging its ability to maintain data locality and define selection criteria without disclosure. We then develop a novel federated extraction protocol, allowing multiple clients to collaboratively determine component dimensions without revealing sensitive information. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of our proposed protocol using synthetic and real-world datasets, including classification and clustering tasks.

In large-scale data-intensive networks, effective content delivery requires not only content storage but also optimal resource allocation to harvesting computational units. We examine a delivery strategy within Named Data Networking frameworks that coordinates content delivery and computing needs in heterogeneous networks supporting both storage and processing of content. We formulate a network utility maximization problem and decompose it into two sub-problems: determining the optimal routing of content and the optimal allocation of computational resources. These sub-problems are efficiently resolved using steepest descent and fractional programming approaches, yielding simple, distributed algorithms with minimal overhead. Notably, these solutions remain robust even in the presence of packet loss and queue management issues, thanks to their stochastic stability and max-min fairness properties. We demonstrate through simulations that these algorithms outperform traditional TCP in terms of Delays, queue lengths, and lower packet retransmissions.

We examine the stability of an extended Euler-Bernoulli beam system consisting of $N \ge 2$ beams connected at a central vertex with no external support. By introducing operational transformation techniques, we derive explicit formulas for the eigenvalues of the associated spectral problem, thereby proving that all eigenvalues are finite.

In the quark-meson model incorporating explicit chiral symmetry breaking, a first-order phase transition is demonstrated, separating nonconducting solid and inhomogeneous conducting phases. The transition involves transitioning from an insulating state with no magnetic field to a state exhibiting periodic magnetization and superconductivity. Furthermore, adding more to the breaking of chiral symmetry results in a second transition, separating insulating and superconducting phases via a Landau-type mechanism, often resulting in vortex lattice formation. Chiral symmetry breaking significantly impacts the transition order, transforming it from a continuous transition between normal and superconducting phases to the described sequence of transitions.

First principles calculations confirm the emergence of strong spin orbit coupling effects in Tl-based topological insulators with the composition MTl4Te3 where M is either Cd or Hg, yielding an opening of the band gap near the Fermi level due to this coupling. The material exhibits characteristics of a topological insulator through the presence of surface states supported by electronic configurations stemming from strong covalent bonding between Cd/Cd and Te atoms, resulting in an energy band at approximately 0.3 eV below the Fermi level. The strong covalent bonding contributes to the stability of the system, with the calculated formation energy being -0.28 eV/atom, and this stability is further enhanced by the entropy gain associated with the material's synthetic process. The desired 1/2 filling condition essential for topological insulator properties is met due to both metal and tellurium atoms contributing to the system's electronic structure. The predicted small but significant band gap of 22 meV is substantial enough to withstand experimental testing, and this research offers a promising pathway for identifying other topological insulators with adjustable formation energies.

Optimizing complex systems often involves adjusting system parameters within a high-dimensional space. When there are multiple objectives to consider, like cost and performance, the optimization process typically involves finding an optimal trade-off. This is often achieved through utility function-based Pareto optimization, where a utility function is used to convert the multi-objective problem into a single-objective one. However, defining this utility function can be challenging, as it's not always clear how to balance the objectives. To address this, we've developed an approach to learn the utility function from expert feedback. By asking experts to compare optimized parameters rather than their scores, we can learn the underlying preference structure more efficiently. To prevent over-fitting and ensure the learned utility function is generalizable, we've introduced a regularization method that leverages existing knowledge about the system. In our setup, we frame the utility function learning as an inverse optimization problem and use constrained tree structures to represent the utility function, which also helps generalization by limiting its complexity. By incorporating knowledge into the utility function, we find that the learned utility function yields better results than one derived solely from the existing system information.

Our proposed blackbox temporalassaults exploit the vulnerability of reinforcement learning agents that rely on approximated temporal information. By taking advantage of the time it takes for these agents to learn the optimal action, we can manipulate their behavior through carefully crafted perturbations. The temporalassaults are particularly effective against agents that use deep Q-networks and model-based reinforcement learning, but can also have a positive influence on the robustness of target policies by forcing them to learn temporally robust features.

Our research delves into the intricate Laping symmetry of a 2D wallpaper lattice, unveiling a novel linear nodal line that exhibits both Lapping and rotational symmetries. The Lapping symmetry, unique to certain two-dimensional lattices, generates multiple nodal lines or a complex network when combined with rotational symmetry. We demonstrate that a simple square lattice model can capture the essential electronic properties of a 2D non-symmorphic lattice with high accuracy. The demonstration of Lapping symmetry, manifested through linear nodal points, is successfully shown in the experimentally synthesized V-shaped dimer network made of 3D-printed rods.

In risk-averse reinforcement learning under non-stationary environments, we investigate the optimal balance between exploration and caution in dynamic settings. The concept risk sensitivity is rigorously explored, starting from the fully observed Markov decision process and progressing to partially observed dynamic systems. Our approach reveals the idiosyncratic nature of each risk-sensitive parameter and overcomes previous limitations that treated these parameters homogeneously. Specifically, we establish novel upper bounds on the dynamic regret for fully observed and partially observed risk-sensitive reinforcement learning models, demonstrating their dependence on the sensitivity parameter and exploring its implications on the sensitivity's asymptotic behavior. Our analysis leads to novel identification strategies that adapt to the sensitivity parameter and leverages the separation design to efficiently decouple value estimation and policy optimization in partially observed settings, ultimately paving the way for a broader understanding of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning under dynamic conditions.

Machine learning models are increasingly used to automate defect resolution by predicting key issues from software development databases, known as issue tracking systems. Most research relies on artificially generated issue tracking datasets, which may not accurately reflect real-world data characteristics. To address this limitation, we developed Substitute Issue Tracking Data, a collection of publicly accessible Jira repositories featuring naturally occurring issue tracking data. By utilizing the available REST API, Substitute Issue Tracking Data can be accessed and integrated into analyses. Our research involved comparing Substitute Issue Tracking Data with traditionally crafted datasets and across all available dataset sources. Our findings reveal significant differences, including variations in entry volume and distribution patterns.

Decentralized training of machine learning models takes into account privacy concerns when models are trained across multiple devices, like servers or data centers, without explicit data sharing. This method gathers aggregated gradient updates from individual devices. Currently, well-known aggregation functions, such as averaging, are used but suffer from slow convergence rates. This is particularly problematic given the large scale of modern datasets and computing devices. This research introduces novel aggregation functions in a new class that includes non-linear functions allowing significantly accelerated convergence rates, up to exponential convergence in some cases, without sacrificing model accuracy. This method can be integrated into existing privacy-preserving distributed ML protocols without modifications, leading to substantial training time reductions and costs in practical applications.

A recent advancement in quantum photonics utilizes trapped single atoms as deterministically placed quantum bits. While recent progress has been made with standalone trapped atoms, the development of compact, scalable devices incorporating single atoms necessitates integrated systems combining atoms with photonic structures. However, the miniaturization of these devices poses significant technical challenges. Our research presents a novel approach utilizing multi-grating technology to efficiently trap, manipulate, and detect single atoms on a photonic chip. This approach employs a series of interconnected waveguides and gratings to trap atoms near a cavity, steer photons emitted by the atom through a series of funnels and decouplers to a collection channel. This innovative design successfully collects over 90% of resonance fluorescence from a trapped rubidium atom via a moving auxiliary atom, and more broadly applies to gravimetry and sensing applications as well.

Let the monoid of finite words, $\Lambda^*$, be defined over an alphabet, $\Lambda$, equipped with a strict order. The set of $\Lambda^*$ completion forms a complete lattice, where the set of convex submonoids constitutes the set of comp elements. The join operation in this completion is related to the MacNeille completion. Given a convex submonoid $N$ and finite words $u$ and $v$, their join with $N$ is equal to the intersection of $N$ with the product of the submonoids generated by $u$ and $v$. The purpose of this paper, where $\Lambda$ is assumed to be strictly ordered, where the first element is the smallest, from the set of convex submonoids of $\Lambda^*$, where the set of finitely generated convex submonoids of $\Lambda^*$ can be characterized based on specific properties. The derived properties enable the explicit computation of the completion element of $N$ from the set of convex submonoids of $\Lambda^*$. The proposed completion method presents an alternative to previously established methods, where the completion of a monoid can be expressed as a quotient of a monoid of finite words. The method's primary advantage is its applicability to any convex submonoid of $\Lambda^*$. The suggested algorithm for computing the completion element relies on determining the syntactic monoid of the convex submonoid in question.

Organic polymers exhibit unique electrical properties that make them suitable for integration into various electronic devices. The molecular structure of these polymers can be manipulated to control their characteristics, but the unknown polymers at our disposal need to beappted for novel applications. The challenge lies in identifying polynuclear molecules based on their unique features. This paper outlines a novel approach that involves using a polymer with adjustable substituents to encode information on linear molecules through the analysis of their absorption spectra at various wavelengths. By applying the principle of integer programming, we are able to determine the most likely molecule from the encoded information. The proposed method has been tested and found to accurately identify all test molecules.

The complexity of medical technology has grown increasingly intricate, making it difficult to analyze using conventional methods. Consequently, there's an urgent need to incorporate human factors into engineering design and research. Researchers in control engineering are utilizing a transcription approach called Direct Transcription (D.T.) to investigate medical applications. Despite its potential benefits, this method has been difficult to adopt due to its perceived complexity. This research paper aims to provide a user-friendly introduction to D.T. through comprehensive computer simulations and step-by-step explanations. Additionally, we provide interactive examples that demonstrate how this approach can be used to analyze and improve medical procedures, ultimately making it more accessible to control engineers. Specifically, we provide a detailed analysis of two patient ventilation strategies during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

Consider a rational map $f$ of degree at least two that has two critical points. We show that there exists a finite number of sets of sequences, each representing different decoding patterns, such that any repeated iteration of $f$ will have cognitive states belonging to one of these sets.

In the context of a linear regression model with high dimensions ($p$) and limited samples ($n$), considering model uncertainty and variance, this paper investigates characteristics (mean, covariance, skewness, kurtosis) of the least squares estimator when the model dimensions ($p$) are on the order of ($n \log n$). Initially, assuming non-stochastic predictors, this paper first establishes empirical Bayes means and covariances using least squares residuals and proves their strong consistency under certain conditions. Subsequently, under assumptions about random response and design matrices, the paper establishes the asymptotic convergence rates for these estimates and similarly proves strong consistency for its kurtosis estimate. Finally, the paper explores the potential applications of these empirical Bayes means, covariances, skewness, and kurtosis in regression analysis.

Bayesian theory provides statistical tools for modeling uncertainty in parameters of interest, typically based on expert knowledge and measurements, allowing us to draw conclusions about these parameters. The use of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to generate samples from posterior distributions is standard, but calculating the resulting distributions can be computationally expensive, making the application of the methods impractical in some cases. Consequently, the methods are rarely utilized for high-dimensional problems. However, the incorporation of the techniques into an energy-efficient machining framework has the potential for significant real-world savings. In response, we have developed a novel approach that leverages the advantages of Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) and the Adaptive Multi-Objective Real-coding Genetic Algorithm (AMOARGA) to achieve this integration. The ABC permits us to derive an approximate Bayesian distribution of cutting parameters, while the AMOARGA enhances the efficiency of sampling from this approximate distribution. Specifically, the algorithm utilizes knowledge from previous generations to refine the sampling process. Simulation results have demonstrated that ABC and AMOARGA can derive an approximate Bayesian distribution of cutting parameters in less time than conventional MCMC methods, thus enabling real-time energy usage estimation of machining centers.

The spectral dimension of a weighted graph is defined by the asymptotic behavior of the weighted negative Laplacian's eigenvalue eigenfunctions. The negative Laplacian of a weighted graph can be viewed as a discrete version of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a metric measure space, where the weights serve as the measure. The aim of this study is to investigate the relationship between the spectral dimension and the Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of weighted finite graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any given weighted finite graph, there exists a probability measure that renders the graph conformally equivalent to one with a probability measure under which its dimension does not exceed the conformal dimension. Furthermore, we find that this is not universally true when the graph is infinite.

Utilizing η-η' mixing to blend the two possible solutions for the mass spectrum, 
we evaluate which one aligns better with observed data. Our analysis incorporates 
considerations of kaon decay into light charmonium states and the variation in mass 
of the η' particle due to mixing with octet and singlet states. This blend reveals 
that the mass spectrum from the linear potential model closely matches experimental 
results, particularly after excluding the η' interaction with the photon.

This study investigates unique online signature templates from 129 participants using ECG electrodes and explores their uniqueness, complexity, and reproducibility. To assess uniqueness, the Hamming distance between templates is measured after classification into distinct groups using the Euclidean distance and a two-step procedure. Following this, the complexity of each template is evaluated through the computation of its complexity index via SOC analysis. Lastly, the reproducibility of the templates is determined by calculating the inter-session and intra-session distances. The results indicate that approximately 60% of the participants provided signatures with 100% uniqueness, approximately 40% yielded groups with unique signatures, the average complexity index for all participants is around 2.5 bits, and both intra-session and inter-session distances exhibit similar distributions.

We investigate the six supersymmetric asymmetric orbifold models to evaluate the impact of higher-derivative corrections on the massless non-BPS states in four-dimensional type II string theory. These models serve as a perfect framework to explore corrections to the massless states due to their simple construction. Our analysis employs the modern light-cone formalism to explicitly verify the existence of corrections corresponding to D'Hoker and Green's proposal of $(s+t+u)^2$. In addition, we explore the relationship between our findings and the hypothesis that all even massless states disappear after taking into account the higher-derivative corrections.

The combination of high mobility and the ability to apply large compressive stresses makes MoS$_2$ an ideal two-dimensional material for investigating moir\'e superlattices. These structures display unique properties arising from interaction between moir\'e bands and electronic spin as well as orbital angular momentum. To explore these characteristics, researchers employed resonant inelastic X-ray scattering to analyze a MoS$_2$ moir\'e superlattice with periodicity of 12 nm, created through strain. This technique revealed multiple excitations within the 0.5 to 1.0 eV energy range, some of which were enhanced when probing with core holes resonant at specific energies. These resonant inelastic X-ray scattering measurements indicated higher-order spin-orbit coupling associated with holes in the valence bands in the presence of localized electron moir\'e pockets. To gain deeper insights, researchers used resonant Raman scattering, obtaining complementary information that supported these findings and provided additional insights into the nature of these associations.

Nitrogen's 14 mass and 7 proton count make it the ideal candidate for a proton-rich freeze-out from a carbon nucleus with six protons, via the slow neutron capture process.  Because of this relationship, it's expected that carbon-rich stars would have less nitrogen than carbon, as it's anticipated that carbon would dominate over both oxygen and nitrogen.  However, this prediction has not been confirmed by the analysis of carbon-rich hypergiants stars through a detailed study of their atmospheric compositions.  The results of this study revealed significant variations in the ratios of carbon to oxygen and carbon to nitrogen, with carbon being neither the dominant nor a smaller component compared to oxygen and nitrogen.  Carbon to nitrogen ratios were found to range widely from approximately 100 to 0.0001.  Carbon-rich stars with higher masses are predicted to experience more efficient neutron capture on 13nitrogen, and the analysis revealed carbon-rich stars with carbon to nitrogen ratios smaller than expected.  The only known mechanism that can explain these findings is if carbon is converted into less carbon isotopes and more nitrogen through interaction with helium in carbon-rich stars, and the carbon to nitrogen ratio is reduced in subsequent stars through efficient neutron capture on 13nitrogen.

Multilingual individuals possess a rich variety of languages that enable them to communicate effectively, but it also complicates natural language processing (NLP) due to complexities in automatically determining the primary language. Although research has progressed in areas like determining the language, reading, and writing directions, significant challenges remain in developing applications for multilingual societies. Multilingual communities often employ a single, code-mixed script for multiple languages, which adds a layer of complexity to NLP tasks. For example, individuals may use English and Hindi to communicate, but with script-based complications, they may use different scripts like Devanagari and Latin. Despite these challenges, multilingual societies like South Asia continue to grow, and it is crucial for NLP research to keep up with these dynamic changes to ensure that technology serves a broader audience.

Biomedical complex graphs provide valuable insights into relationships among various entities.
Biomedical DL models have the potential to create visual representations of intricate graph patterns,
which can then be employed to forecast missing links and detect anomalies.
This would enhance human comprehension and decision-making capabilities in the biomedical field.
To achieve this, we introduce GDELM, a Dep depiction learning model for complex graph completion,
which identifies and depictions of intricate patterns within a graph that contribute to the completion of missing edges.
Unlike traditional node-based learning models, GDELM captures the intricate interconnections among nodes and edges,
producing both high-performance and interpretable results.
We evaluate our model on two datasets and demonstrate its superiority to state-of-the-art methods,
demonstrating its capacity to depict complex patterns that aid in predicting missing edges.

Our research utilizes enhanced white dwarfs as indirect detectors to set the most stringent limits to date on the properties of WIMPs and SU(2)$_L\times$SU(2)$_R$ left-right symmetric models (LRSM). For WIMPs with masses under 30 GeV, our new limits surpass those from other direct and indirect detection methods, particularly in the case of multiple, possible WIMP dark matter annihilation channels. In models based on LRSM, our enhanced white dwarf models surpass the best limits obtained from multiple processes with cross sections below those predicted by the standard model. Specifically, our new constraints on the XR parameter in LRSM models are the strictest ever obtained, rendering virtually impossible the complete replacement of WIMPs by stable particles in this type of model.

Shared data breaches can cause significant harm to individual privacy, an issue that existing tools fail to address effectively. Although graph data analysis has made substantial strides in predicting data sharing risks, previous methods primarily focused on structural information and overlooked content-driven features. To bridge this gap, we introduce GraphPrivacy, a system comprising visual aids and an automated engine that evaluates data graphs based on both structural and content-related characteristics to estimate data sharing risks. Through thorough evaluations on publicly available datasets and collaborations with real-world experts, we demonstrate that GraphPrivacy's structural and content-driven risk assessment mechanisms outperform existing techniques, with practitioners praising the approach's accuracy and highlighting improvements possible through refined feature selection.

Butler and Regev previously established a one-to-one correspondence between specific convex geometric models and pure complexes in a category of concave sheaves. Building upon this foundation, we explore alternative frameworks for these geometric models. Firstly, we develop a new representation for concealed purity by leveraging the symmetry inherent in the convex geometric models. Additionally, we propose an alternative definition for concealed purity based on high-level properties of pure complexes. Our approach is then applied to the context of sheaves on analytic spaces.

This study compares the fragmentation characteristics of hadrons produced in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC. Using measurements from the ATLAS detector, analyses were conducted for both gluon- and quark-dominated jet samples across a range of collision energies. In proton-proton collisions, observed ratios of fragmented gluons to quarks were found to match expectations based on perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics simulations, with certain exceptions at lower momentum values. Notably, quenching observations in heavy-ion collisions showed that gluons and quarks lose energy at different rates. Data were obtained from $pp$ and Pb+Pb collisions at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 5.02 TeV. Jets with high momentum values were analysed, with corresponding leading fragment functions derived and compared to theoretical DGLAP evolution models.

The CP2K program package, often listed among top scientific applications, excels in hybrid density functional theory and quantum molecular dynamics simulations. Its prowess spans multiple disciplines including chemistry, physics, and materials science. Tailing behind the efficiency of its counterparts by only a factor of two, recent advancements have narrowed this gap. With the impending exascale computing capabilities, utilizing systems with millions of processing units presents both an exciting opportunity and a formidable challenge. Our recent contributions have facilitated the seamless operation of CP2K at such large scales, leveraging both Anton and manycore architectures. This manuscript outlines the specific modifications made to enable CP2K's functionality on these systems and discusses the outcomes attained thus far.

Researchers examined the most subtle, intense $1\text{-}1.5\,\AA$ solar coronal X-ray brightenings detected by the Focusing X-ray Spectrometer (FOXSI) instrument between 2015 and 2019. Despite being significantly below the Coronal H-alpha Spectrometer (CHX-S) threshold of $5\times10^4\,\mathrm{cm}^{-6}\,\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1}\,\mathrm{sr}^{-1}$, these observations revealed the presence of Coronal H-alpha Emission (CHE) sources. Two out of the observed events coincided with Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), exhibiting maximum intensities of $3.5\times10^4$ and $2.8\times10^4$, while a third event reached a maximum intensity of $1.9\times10^4$. Despite these lower than expected values, they suggest that detecting CHE may become feasible with upgraded capabilities of the upgraded FOXSI-3.

Graph neural networks excel in processing complex real-world data, but often struggle with reliability due to issues like missing data, noise, and underrepresentation of certain categories. This problem is exacerbated when assessing the impact of certain social groups on system performance. Graph data enhancement techniques can help mitigate these challenges by improving data quality and quantity, both prior to and during model training. By leveraging these techniques, we can accurately measure the social impact of AI technologies by expanding and diversifying available data. This research demonstrates the utility of these methods in real-world data analysis and code availability can be found at https://github.com/wenweiliu2000/SI-GNN.

The dimension of the conformal field theory's representation space corresponds to the dimension of the Heisenberg equation solution space, which in turn equals the number of variables in the Heisenberg equation. By applying a well-established method from mathematical control theory, we compute the controllability of the Heisenberg equation using the Euler-Arnold equation and demonstrate its correspondence to the conformal field theory's intricacy, measured by the tensor network depth of the conformal waveform. Furthermore, we successfully derive the exact solution of the Heisenberg equation through the Euler-Arnold equation and map its mapping time to the tensor network depth, as well as to the circuit model's mapping time in eigenvalue problems in quantum computing. In addition, we use this approach to calculate the intricacy of various eigenvalue problems and obtain new insights into the eigenvalue solving process in quantum computing.

Pose estimation in high-dimensional spaces remains a crucial yet unresolved challenge across various fields like biomedical and industrial applications. Traditional techniques often struggle with reliability and completeness, particularly in handling data noise and real-world constraints. We present an efficient and robust method called CompleteLS, designed to accurately estimate pose in high-dimensional spaces using data noise-resilient Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs). Complementing CompleteLS is an optimized state-of-the-art solver, GOptSTAP, which leverages complete model estimates to determine the optimal transformation parameters via iterative optimization and continuous relaxation. CompleteLS and GOptSTAP work in tandem to ensure reliable and complete pose estimation with optimized performance. Our results confirm that CompleteLS is comparable to leading methods in terms of efficiency and further demonstrate its accuracy and completeness under optimized transformation parameters.

The hidden sector hypothesis suggests there may be dark matter connected to hidden sectors with their own unique properties and interaction strengths. We investigate the possibility of dark matter being linked to hidden sectors that led to a universe with separate temperatures for visible and hidden matter in the early universe. A 3-1 MeV hidden sector exit time is required to produce the observed densities of dark and ordinary matter, which would also introduce new constraints on this dark matter candidate due to its interaction with hydrogen. We demonstrate that the hydrogen 21-cm signal can potentially rule out 3-1 MeV hidden sector models in order to match the matter density we observe in the universe. We propose that a hydrogen line emission boost, as indicated by recent research, could be an indication of a future multitemperature universe.

Researchers have detected W boson pairs with the same sign at the Large Hadron Collider, attributed to electroweak production processes. A total of 23.3 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data, collected at a 13 TeV energy level, was analyzed to study these events. An examination was conducted to distinguish visible signatures among different production methods by analyzing the masses of pairs of jets and focusing on the angles between these particles. A significant breakthrough occurred when researchers detected the contribution of direct production techniques among these events beyond statistical variations, detectable through analyses of detached event signatures. Joint probabilities reject various theoretical models at 95% confidence levels with maximum cross-section limits of 34, 26, and 24 fb respectively for monophoton toponium, dimuon toponium, and charged Higgs boson pair production at a 13 TeV energy level, in addition to improved constraints on weakly interacting massive particle parameters with coupling λtilde χ^0 χ^+ of -0.04 to 0.04 fb and a bound of -0.04 to 0.04 fb. An examination was conducted to study visible signatures among events beyond statistical variations, detectable through analyses of detached event signatures. This work tackles the challenge of enhancing color information in monochromatic images captured by cameras with distinct color filters. Existing color translation approaches are limited to cameras with the same optical setup, resulting in inaccurate colors when applied across different models. Our solution involves transferring color profiles between various cameras by calculating and fine-tuning a transform based on raw monochromatic images and known color calibration data. Our method can be applied without access to reference information from other cameras and yields precise color reconstructions, leading to improved vividness and saturation in final color images.

Our re-analysis of the Planck 2015 data reveals a discrepancy between the observed angular spectrum of temperature and polarized temperature anisotropies and the predictions of the standard $\Lambda$CDM$` model, specifically a $1\sigma$ deviation in $A_L/A_L\LambdaCDM$ and a $2\sigma$ deviation in $\Gamma\Gamma/\Gamma\Gamma\LambdaCDM$ when comparing the quadrature sum of uncertainties to the model predictions. This analysis identifies the most significant discrepancies occurring between redshifts of $z=3$ and $z=30$, and explores multiple potential explanations for the discrepancy, including non-standard recombination physics and early integration of dark matter. Moreover, the uncertainty associated with $A_L$ decreases with higher precision in recombination calculations, suggesting that future improvements in this area could further investigate the discrepancy's origin.

The rapid expansion of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven an surge in research on LLM maintenance, yet most models remain confined to conventional modification strategies, overlooking innovative maintenance methods discovered among contributors on platforms like GitHub. Our study delves into this overlooked area, uncovering unconventional but effective methods such as reusing, merging, and temporarily relocating code snippets to streamline maintenance processes, known as meta-maintenance operations. We have developed a method to detect these operations and created a dataset consisting of 533,119 PRs where meta-maintenance operations were employed, representing approximately 2% of all GitHub PRs. Our findings reveal that these operations are often employed to enhance or consolidate code snippets, and while they pose potential risks, their systematic application can improve the efficiency and quality of software maintenance.

The eclipsing binary BD And has been the subject of debate, with observations conflicting and challenging its proposed status as a pair of stars with varying periods. The discovery of a candidate Gamma Doradus variability in BD And has been found and confirmed using data from the TESS mission. Analysis using the TESS light curve and other data suggests that the BD And system consists of multiple components, including a third body, and that the observed eclipses are consistent with a binary system with specific star sizes and densities. The consensus is that the BD And system is composed of stars with periods matching that of the TESS data and that any previously proposed fourth member is unnecessary to explain the observed variability. The stars in BD And have been found to have masses and radii consistent with typical BD And system parameters, with the consensus being that BD And is best described as a binary system with periods matching that of the TESS data.

This paper has a two-part objective. Firstly, it establishes the existence and uniqueness of global, smooth solutions to the fractional Yamabe flow, expressed as $\partial_t u = c_n^{\beta} \Delta^{\beta}(u^{p})$, with constraints $1 < \beta < 2$ and $1 < p < 1+\frac{2\beta}{n}$. The initial condition is given by $u(x,0) = u_0(x)$, where $u_0$ is assumed to be even, $u_0 \in H^{2\beta}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with compact support, and belongs to the positive cone of $H^{2\beta}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The proof leverages techniques from the theory of parabolic equations and Scalfino's theory of K-semiconcave and K-convex functions to ensure smoothness of the solution. The paper then investigates the long-term asymptotic behavior of the solution with respect to $t$.

Recent recommendations have shifted towards considering multiple sparse domains to capture comprehensive user preferences across various aspects like products and categories. However, simply aggregating users' interests from different domains may lead to inaccurate or incomplete learning. To address this, we have developed Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDC Rec), which employs multi-task learning to collaborate on multiple sparse domains and effectively learn users' comprehensive aspect preferences. In addition, MSDC Rec integrates the collaborative signals from different data sources, combining the users' interests in products and categories through a unified framework. Furthermore, to handle the incomplete nature of data, we have integrated both implicit and explicit regularization into our model. In comparison to current state-of-the-art methods, evaluation of our approach on two datasets demonstrates superior cooperative recommendation performance.

We establish that under specific conditions, the deformation theory of orthogonal and symplectic bundles can be fully described by $H^1(\mathcal X, \mathfrak{end}(\mathcal M))$, the first hypercohomology group with respect to $\mathfrak{end}(\mathcal M)$. This end morphism sheaf is defined as the kernel of the sheaf $\mathcal Hom(\mathcal M,\mathcal M) \to \mathcal Hom(\mathcal M,\mathcal M(-2))$. Our method involves demonstrating the deformation equivalence of sheaf pairs consisting of isotonicity and monomorphisms, specifically in the case of isotonicity sheaves. This finding allows us to obtain precise descriptions of the local deformation theory for orthogonal and symplectic bundles and leads to additional corollaries regarding the deformation theory of sheaves consisting of orthogonal and symplectic bundles and isotonicities.

Let A(n,k) denote the count of portions of size divisible by k in every partition of n into parts with less than k occurrences. In this study, recursive formulas and sums involving the generalized Bernoulli numbers and Stirling numbers are used to determine the recurrence relationships for A(n,k).

Given $N$ randomly chosen samples from a $D$-dimensional unit ball, where each sample includes $N/2$ uniformly distributed positions and corresponding values that adhere to a smooth function plus noise with magnitude σ, our research demonstrates that any continuous function $f$ with a certain smoothness level can be approximately reconstructed if N grows rapidly enough relative to D and σ. Furthermore, this reconstruction can be achieved through least squares approximation on a suitable polynomial system if N is sufficiently large relative to D and σ. We also initiate exploration into the approximation of highly smooth functions despite noisy data by introducing a novel approach grounded in statistical learning theory. We also derive an error estimate for least squares approximation with noisy data using specific probability bounds that are particularly beneficial when sample sizes are extremely high relative to noise levels.

Recent data from LHC experiments have provided significant insights into the movement of the upper and lower production partson distributions, $u$ and $c$, as well as the carrier distribution, $s$, of the $J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$ and $B_c$ productions. In contrast to $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ productions which follow the pattern of quarkonium movements aligned with the LHC evolution pattern, the $B_c$ production pattern remains unclear due to its complexity and the lack of a consensus on how to apply the movement model to it. Additionally, the movement model of the X(3872) production does not match its expected behavior based on experimental evidence.

Within the disordered Hubbard model, we investigate how disorder impacts quantum critical phenomena, utilizing both numerical findings and analytical arguments. It is demonstrated through numerical evidence that dissorder can lead to the separation of the lower and upper parts of the density of states already present in the non-interacting system ($U=0$). By employing an analytical approach, we investigate the implications of this disorder-induced split, and identify that it can give rise to singular exponent behavior, which contrasts with the universal behavior of the non-disordered Kondo lattice model. We observe that these exponents change gradually with disorder level, but certain attributes, such as power-law decay in density of states below the Fermi energy, do not disappear completely. The obtained results can be described through a real-space renormalization group based on the singlet formation process, which is illustrated through numerical data. This method also allows for the investigation of other quantities, such as the shortest singlet length, which is found to decrease significantly with increased disorder level.

The set of Coxeter elements in a Coxeter group, particularly in the type $A_{n-1}$, possesses a distinctive characteristic: it is the unique minimal set among all conjugates with respect to the length of the elements. Research has shown that this property holds true for the extended $A_{n}$ Coxeter group as well, including the Coxeter group of the Dynkin diagram $A_{n}^{(1)}$. In a study involving the finite $A_{n}$ Coxeter group, the length of elements within each conjugate class has been explored, utilizing this research, a new proof for the foundation theorem of the $A_{n}$ Coxeter group, distinct from the previously established proof, has been established. Furthermore, the nature of the length of the Coxeter elements has been confirmed, acting as a key factor in the alternative proof of the foundation theorem.

Solitons in interacting scalar field theories, when there's no $SO(2)$ invariance, were previously deemed impossible based on an old argument. However, we discovered that such solitons can actually exist within the broader context of non-$SO(2)$ invariant theories. We constructed a specific model that supports both stable particle solitons and reflective domain walls. This discovery has significant implications for various fields, including inflationary cosmology, where the universe may be part of a higher-dimensional space that includes field theories lacking $SO(2)$ invariance. It's also possible that some of the dark matter we observe today consists of these stable particle solitons.

Recent advancements in inverse reinforcement learning techniques have been significant, 
with many models now available that can learn agent goals from expert behavior and subsequent actions. 
However, these approaches struggle with complex environments requiring prolonged learning and may be inaccurate given the large volume of data needed. 
Furthermore, they are ill-equipped to handle partially-regulated environments where only a subset of the overall goals influences an agent's behavior. 
To address these limitations, we suggest a novel, time-efficient Hierarchical Bayesian model for Inverse RL in partially-regulated settings. 
This model leverages multiple layers of tasks, each with varying degrees of influence, and can be efficiently solved using the Expectation Maximization algorithm. 
Our model has undergone extensive evaluation with both simulated and real-world datasets, 
demonstrating superior performance and scalability compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Let X and Y be locally compact Hausdorff spaces, with Y containing at least two points. If every continuous map from X to Y is constant, then either Y is compact, or the image of any continuous map from X to the deformation target of Y under the deformation functor is also constant.

Reinforcement learning offers an effective method for addressing complex control problems, yet it's frequently hindered by stability issues in practical applications. These stability challenges often necessitate control experts' deep knowledge to simplify and resolve problems, thereby limiting broader adoption. By leveraging deep reinforcement learning's ability to learn challenging problems through visual features in state observations, our approach aims to enhance adoption rates. By employing a two-staged deep reinforcement learning technique, our method successfully refines exploratory behavior into strategic policies without relying on expert simplifications. As a result, we've achieved stable solutions for multiple high-difficulty control problems and will explore the underlying principles of state representation, action evaluation, and policy learning through this approach.

This study is part of a series focusing on the evolution of black hole mass distributions across the universe's history using semi-analytical models. By simulating the entire universe, researchers were able to investigate when very heavy black holes (over 10^5 solar masses) first appeared, how their distribution changes over time, and the impact of early black hole formation on galaxy development. Two different models for the formation of seeds, one producing lighter seeds (100 solar masses) and the other heavier ones (1000 solar masses), were simulated in an established galaxy formation model to understand the impact of early black hole mass on final distributions. Both seed models resulted in final black hole masses exceeding 10^9 solar masses by z=0, but only the heavier seed model accurately predicted the masses observed in the centers of massive galaxies. This suggests that heavy seeds require extreme environment to grow into very massive black holes, while lighter models typically result in black holes in galaxy-formed systems fall within the mass range observed.

To maximize the benefits of machine learning in scientific research, models must not only be efficient but also interpretable and able to provide clear, accurate predictions. In this study, we demonstrate the capabilities of Gaussian process regression using the \texttt{gprknn} package in R to handle large inelastic neutron scattering datasets. By utilizing publicly available data, we show that this approach can effectively smooth noisy data, identify and display key resonance patterns, and provide precise statistical measurements of fitted parameters such as mean predictions, uncertainties, and correlation coefficients.

In the past thirty years, preprints have dramatically altered the research publication landscape by facilitating and transforming how scholars disseminate and disseminate their findings. Before preprints, scholars relied solely on print media to disseminate their research, which then supplemented existing publication databases with online preprint services in the 1990s. As a result, an exponential increase in the number of preprints occurred, ultimately leading to a 20-fold surge within the last three decades. This surge was both the result of scientists' need for more efficient research dissemination and a self-fulfilling prophecy that science would eventually be dominated by preprints. This study delves into the variety of preprint models that exist today and how they provide different types of solutions to the dissemination of research, thereby offering scientists more choice and control.

This laboratory journal offers a unified solution for model experimentation,
electronic data collection and analysis, all attainable within a single notebook
by applying the concept of 'quasi-pure functions'. The methodology is inspired
by functional programming but implemented using a minimal set of Python
constructs - list comprehensions, calling without argument evaluation (*args),
the sent expression and the do-while loop - to mimic the behavior of 'lazy
evaluation'. The methodology's efficacy is demonstrated with two real-world
cases: first, a simulation of an electronic circuit to model the behavior of a
do-while loop; second, the control and collection of data from laboratory
equipment via serial port using *args.

High-entropy alloys have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their exceptional performance capabilities. These advanced materials can be created using various structures, from ordered and dual-phase to amorphous forms, achieved through the careful selection of multiple constituent elements. High-entropy alloys exhibit exceptional strength, exceptional temperature resistance, exceptional corrosion resistance, and exceptional wear resistance. The incorporation of machine learning techniques has significantly accelerated the development of these exceptional materials, enhancing their potential applications in aerospace, medical devices, nuclear components, and advanced tools. This article delves into the rapid advancement of high-entropy alloys, explores the successful application of machine learning in these materials, and outlines the future opportunities and challenges they present.

The exploration of the $T_{cc}^+$ bottomonium molecule leads to a prediction 
regarding an underlying atomic partner, which we denote as $X_{cc}^+$. This $X_{cc}^+$ 
particle decays into a $D^{\ast+}D^-$ and $D^{\ast-}D^+$ pair. Moreover, its interactions 
with $D^{\ast \pm}$ and $D0$ particles are explored. Utilizing large-$N_c$ and 
quark-model frameworks allows us to make several predictions about this $X_{cc}^+$. 
Notably, its size is comparable to that of $D^{\ast-}D^-$-space, and it does not 
exhibit the same large spatial extent as $T_{cc}^+$. Furthermore, we anticipate 
a notably narrower decay of $X_{cc}^+$ into a $D^{\ast+}D^-$ pair in comparison 
to the $T_{cc}^+$'s analogous decay.

Machine learning models with predefined parameters can benefit from defining a set of possible outcomes, which we refer to as the latent state space. This concept applies across various domains, including graphical neural networks and the dynamics of differential equations. Our goal is to create a unified approach to defining the probabilistic outcome pool for defining these models' latent spaces, by defining the rate of transition between different states in the latent space as the result of a differential equation or random chance. This unified approach enables the use of current graphical neural networks and defines the latent state space in a manner that accommodates various types of latent variable models, such as those defined by differential equations and probabilistic models with a set of possible states. Our method enables the implicit definition of the latent space without explicitly defining its structure. This approach enables the efficient training of graphical neural networks using current optimization techniques and defines the latent state space in a manner that accommodates various types of models, such as those defined by differential equations and chance-based models.

Recently, Li et al. and Tang et al. created diverse families of APN functions using geometric approaches, but it is known that their functions are merely super weakly nonlinear. We contribute to this field by defining and utilizing the concept of slim Sidon sets to establish a broader class of non-linear functions with a higher degree of nonlinearity. Furthermore, we combine this new class with existing families to create hybrid functions, and prove through induction that many of these functions are complete non-linear.

Binary matrix annotation often involves extensive time consumption due to 
the need for expert review. This process can be streamlined by applying samples 
to the available experts, taking into account that some specialists may be expert 
in certain subjects but others in different. In this work, we tackle the problem 
of subjecting binary matrices to various sampling procedures that can be tailored 
to the given constraints, including those that are subject to specific row and column 
sums, and exploring different non-uniform sampling strategies. Additionally, we 
present an efficient method for achieving any desired binary matrix distribution 
while adhering to fixed row and column sums, and demonstrate the applicability of 
these sampling techniques on real-world datasets from the fields of biology and social sciences.

Precision in measuring differential cross sections is crucial for constraining current parton distribution function models, yet existing cross section models are plagued by substantial uncertainties, especially at low $x$ and low $Q^2$ values. As LHC and non-leptonic weak interaction experiments generate vast amounts of high-precision data, parton distribution function uncertainties are becoming a major limitation in interpreting these findings. To overcome this issue, global parton distribution function fits are being revised to incorporate all data and minimize biases, with new frameworks such as the RT-Framework facilitating this process by incorporating user-friendly parts of the RTM framework.

This document details the latest open-source release of the ELKI data mining framework, specifically version 0.7.5, also known as 'Heidelberg'. It serves as a comprehensive, multi-paradigm, and domain-agnostic Java package featuring an extensive array of data analysis tools and algorithms. The document provides an overview of the framework, its key capabilities, and future plans, accompanied by supporting release notes, including notable enhancements, new functionalities, modifications, and deletions across various components of the framework.

We introduce a novel approach to planting an optical frequency comb within microresonators using multiple, carefully timed pump pulses. These pulses initiate and sustain the comb's generation by activating a sequence of pulse cycles. This technique offers enhanced control over comb properties including its threshold, pulse shape, stability, extinction ratio, and spectral power. A specially designed microresonator utilizing nematic liquid crystals enabled a study demonstrating the efficiency of this approach, achieving an extinction ratio exceeding 20 dB at a pump power of 14 W.
