If the category functions generate a central von Neumann algebra, we demonstrate that it can be centrally decomposed into a direct integral of type I factors. Furthermore, if the category functions are massive, we show they produce a factor. This analysis also leads to a new proof of the center being finite for sl₂.

In this study, a modified value iteration scheme has been developed that generates an interval containing the optimal value function of large-scale discrete time Markov decision processes. Building upon the concept of imprecise arithmetic, this modification transforms the standard policy iteration method into a set of linear system solves using interval analysis. An adjusted GMRES algorithm is employed to compute an inexact policy iteration sequence, which has been demonstrated under certain conditions to converge towards the optimal value function. Numerical evaluations have been conducted to assess the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach.

Consider a weighted directed graph $\mathcal{D}$ and the edge ideal $I_{\mathcal{D}}$. We will demonstrate the simplicity of computing typical and symbolic powers of $I_{\mathcal{D}}$ under certain weighted directed graph conditions. Additionally, a method will be proposed to calculate typical and symbolic powers of $I_{\mathcal{D}}$ for oriented bipartite graphs using a specific algebraic approach and a graph-theoretic result, respectively, ultimately enabling the computation of typical and symbolic powers in this context.

In computer-based experiments, generating valuable data from computer simulations is expedited by using high-speed hardware and advanced software, but the associated costs of multiple runs can be prohibitive. As a result, the simulation inputs and outputs are often too disparate to have a direct relationship. Designing an input space that maximizes information gain in such scenarios poses significant challenges, especially when the goal is to identify output values that meet specific criteria within a certain range. This study develops a novel algorithm that optimizes an estimated criterion range by fitting a user-defined contour to the Pareto frontier of an estimated probability distribution function. By demonstrating its efficacy on various functions, the approach's versatility is highlighted even in the absence of an underlying mathematical function, making it applicable to various functions with different characteristics.

Making reliable decisions in uncertain environments is a major challenge. People often seek assistance when exploring their surroundings to help them learn and adapt. Traditionally, help has been assumed to be global, the same for all learning scenarios. However, it's also possible to obtain assistance on a more individualized basis, tailored to each inquiry. We are interested in understanding under what conditions the ability to request specific types of help leads to more efficient learning. We developed a robust learning framework that allows for targeted inquiries about the most likely scenario at any given point in time and found that this setup allows for more effective learning compared to receiving consistent help throughout the environment. Notably, learning becomes significantly faster compared to getting global help on all scenarios. We further explored the robust value of this targeted inquiry approach and found that while it offers significant benefits, its robust advantage is limited to one additional sample when compared to global inquiries.

For the first time, fragmentation changes in jets have been observed within the QCD medium created in high-energy collisions with a lone photon, using data collected at 5.02 TeV. This discovery is significant because it allows researchers to isolate initial conditions of the formed medium at the point of collision. Data show that alterations in the distribution of particles created alongside high-energy jets change significantly with increasing central force collisions. Additionally, these changes do not change when normalized by the energy of the jets, pointing to fragmentation changes within the medium rather than modifications outside of it.

Building upon previous research involving generalizations of Ap\'{e}ry's famous series for $\zeta(3)$, we develop a new, comprehensive formula that can yield our earlier findings as well as novel identities related to weight w multiple zeta values, especially in cases where w is Witten's characteristic weight of 18 or a multiple of it. This new finding represents a more universal version of the identity originally discovered by Ap\'{e}ry. Furthermore, we develop analogous formulas for the squared generalized Ap\'{e}ry series, yielding analogous generalizations to the identities originally discovered by Ap\'{e}ry himself.

Recent research has now identified WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, also known as "The Mishap" and previously "Mr. Misunderstanding," as a binary brown dwarf pair connected by a tenuous gaseous and dusty stream. WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 (component A) has approximate properties of 14000 years in age, a temperature of approximately 2600 K, and a mass of about 0.084 M_sun, whereas component B has an estimated brightness 1.2 magnitudes greater than A. Both objects exhibit line broadening approximately twice the typical value, potentially due to rotation or motion within the stream. It is hypothesized that A and B are in an unstable binary system undergoing mass loss through a stream that may eventually lead to the formation of a protoplanetary object.

This paper presents the initial results for the production of various light mesons and pions, kaons, proton, antiproton and phi-mesons over a wide range of transverse momentum in Xe-Xe collisions at a nucleon pair center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV, based on data collected by the ALICE experiment at the LHC in 2016. We analyze the rapidity distribution and the rapidity density ratio relative to proton-proton collisions, and also examine the nuclear modification factor as a function of transverse momentum, rapidity and mass. Our findings reveal significant differences between the density of these particles in mini-collisions compared to proton-proton collisions at the same centurial energy, and also suggests that mini-collisions may lead to the creation of conditions that mimic a quark-gluon plasma.

A novel approach is presented to determine the x-dependence of parton distribution functions at an unspecified scale within the QCD framework by utilizing only the x^2-dependent PDF x-dependence at a particular reference scale and the PDFs at multiple reference scales at the same x value. The proposed method relies on the assumption that parton distributions can be effectively parameterized by separating x and alpha_s dependencies as f(x, alpha_s) = A(x) + B(x) alpha_s + C(x) alpha_s^2. The validity of this assumption is examined using data from the pyevosf code and observations that the A(x) and B(x) coefficients exhibit minimal scale variations. The effectiveness of this interpolation method in reconstructing PDFs across different scales is demonstrated, including results for xscheme PDFs intermediate to MS-bar and MS-bar prime scales provided by the DUET2xS scheme. The approach is further applicable to evolve leading-order LO and next-to-leading-order NLF PDFs although such application necessitates the incorporation of additional constraints on scale-dependent higher-order corrections beyond the A and B coefficients.

Space exploration missions beyond low Earth orbit present a significant construction challenge due to the lack of skilled labor and costly life support systems. An in-situ resource of processed planetary regolith can mitigate these constraints if utilized in construction projects. Experimental methods have been developed to create printed structures using complex shapes of meteoritic and lunar soil without necessitating additional life support for the crew. These structures were achieved through the use of heat and pressure to process material and molded into shapes using a custom 3D printer. Mechanical stress tests and examination of samples through microscopes revealed that higher temperatures improved the material's physical properties, resulting in dense and solid samples with distinct grain boundaries. Additionally, the surface of samples showed distinct layering, and those with higher sintering temperatures exhibited finer and more compact features. These findings suggest that regolith from Mars and the Moon can be used to create built structures through in-situ resource management strategies, utilizing limited on-site life support for the crew.

The dynamics of a liquid layer forming beads on a fibre are studied, where the liquid layer's interaction with the fibre is enhanced by slip. This study uses Drazin's theory and modified dispersion relations to predict the rate of instability onset and final bead radius. Simulation results confirm the theoretical predictions in various limits, showing that increased slip enhances the breakup process and results in smaller beads.

We have investigated star formation rates in nearby galaxies by utilizing archival HST data and recent JWST observations focusing on the emission at 4.6 $\mu$m and 2.2 $\mu$m respectively. By using a modified version of the MALT90 star formation rate indicator, which is sensitive to SFR down to $10^{-4} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, we have found that including the emission at 4.6 $\mu$m significantly enhances its lower SFR limit. Furthermore, we have found that the ratio of this 4.6 $\mu$m emission to the 2.2 $\mu$m emission is directly proportional to SFR, which suggests a more accurate and precise method for calculating SFR. This new approach has been validated and cross-referenced with other MALT90 SFR determinations from the $[5.6]/[3.4]$ and Brackett-$\gamma/[3.4]$ ratios. We have also observed that the $L_{dust}/L_{star}$ ratio is both constant and is Ism-independent, which suggests a more reliable method for cross-checking SFRs derived from different methods.

This is the initial publication in a two-part series exploring a broader concept of type $II$ quantum subgroups within the category of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ highest weight modules, referred to as contextual quantum subgroups. These are defined by the presence of a symmetry group acting on regional modules, specifically the tensor product of two modules. It is required that the group preserves the 'relative' weights of the modules. The first publication introduces defines these symmetries and their connections to the Brylinski-Kostant-Grothendieck spectral sequence, while also providing illustrative quantum subgroup examples. The second publication will then proceed to investigate the subgroup's properties.

The diffusion of an asset's price follows a process described by a stochastic differential equation, with its statistical properties determined by the drift and diffusion coefficients. This study delves into the theoretical aspects of the general diffusion model, with a primary objective of determining the broadest class of functions capable of accurately describing the price distribution function, typically characterized by parameters such as mean reversion, skewness, and kurtosis. Complementing this, the paper also investigates the identification of the model's parameters based on empirical data, specifically the first four discrete moments. We present various methods for parameter estimation and evaluate their efficacy, ultimately discovering that the method employing minimum entropy seems to have potential for practical application.

Handwritten mathematical expressions are an essential form of human communication.
However, accurately recognizing them is a complex task due to the variations in
how people write, their writing speeds, and the use of sloppy handwriting and
special tools. An alternative approach involves detecting these expressions from
data obtained from sensors attached to the hands, as it simplifies the recognition
problem by providing consistent input. In this work, we explore this challenge and
propose a framework for classifying mathematical expressions from sensor data.
The method involves segmenting writing sequences and segmenting individual numbers
and symbols, followed by training a neural network to identify mathematical
expressions given these sequences. Experiments are conducted on sensor data created
by training people to write on special boards, with results showing a 66% accuracy in
recognizing the written expressions.

The duration of speech segments significantly influences the effectiveness of connectionist models, particularly in predicting phonetic duration. Traditionally, this duration is estimated using time-aligned data, yet such information is often scarce or absent. While models can still be trained without this data, the reliability of their predictions is compromised, leading to suboptimal performance. Although some research has attempted to create synthetic durations without aligned data, these approaches have limitations stemming from the need to estimate acoustic and spectral parameters. In contrast, this paper proposes a novel framework for generating synthetic durations based on median analysis, eliminating the necessity for such estimations and only requiring speech waveform analysis. Extensive experiments were conducted on the corpus with aligned data to validate the proposed approach, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods and the ability to enhance models' performance when integrated with speech recognition systems.

Species occupancy analysis serves as a widely-adopted initial step in ecological research.
The increasing availability of citizen science data through presence-absence surveys has enabled complex spatial presence models, taking into account spatial autocorrelation and unobserved species.
To address these advancements, the spOccupancy package in R was created to integrate spatial presence models for both single-species and community-level analyses, as well as specialized models for various applications.
This package incorporates Bayesian analysis tools within R and leverages the 'JAGS' functionality.
Our objective is to enhance the accessibility of these methods through features like automatic model compilation, optimized compilation, dynamic runs, and improved starting values to expedite convergence.
Key functionalities are available for handling imperfect detection, integrating covariates, conducting model comparison, model prediction, and performing diagnostic assessments.
Furthermore, we provide built-in functions for computing the Effective Sample Size and correlation structure, facilitating diagnostic analysis.
Our package also enables the creation of response curves, random effect visualization, and predictive mapping within R.
By implementing these methods, researchers can conduct integrated spatial presence modeling independently within R.

Malignant skin lesions require prompt diagnosis to prevent spread. While dermatologists can accurately diagnose these cases, many patients wait excessively long times to see one, leading to delayed diagnosis. Telemedicine has filled this gap with conventional methods using conventional photography and computer-aided diagnosis systems. However, these systems often fall short by failing to leverage the expertise of dermatologists and the capabilities of deep learning for accurate diagnosis. A new cooperative model could combine the strengths of human expertise and artificial intelligence to improve skin lesion diagnosis and accuracy. The proposed Skincare initiative uses a cutting-edge interactive system that enables dermatologists to train deep learning models and automated diagnostic systems through feedback in a virtual setting. We demonstrate its effectiveness by creating a model with skin lesion images and expert input, showcasing improved accuracy and consistency in dermatologists' diagnoses. The Skincare initiative promises to enhance patient care and drive innovation in dermatology by facilitating collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence.

Type Ia supernovae serve as essential tools in cosmology due to their uniform brightness, allowing them to accurately gauge cosmic distances when combined with photometric and spectral light curve analysis. Recent findings suggest that using spectral temporal information can yield more precise distance estimates and Hubble constant measurements. However, current methods relying on principal component analysis and factor analysis are deterministic and may not fully leverage the unique characteristics of each supernova. To address this, we present a probabilistic autoencoder approach that temporarily encodes individual supernovae before encoding the entire dataset, preserving dynamic information in the process. Our model outperforms factor analysis in recovering original signals from noise and surpasses it in reconstructing simulated Type Ia supernovae light curves.

A high-redshift galaxy, exhibiting significant galaxy mass, is observed with a gravitational lens, enhancing our detection of a neutral gas outflow. Our multi-epoch observations using CO emission lines, detected via JWST and ALMA, reveal a neutral gas outflow flowing perpendicular to the outflow plane. This outflow has a velocity of approximately 550-600 km/s and resides at a distance of about 1.5-2.5 kpc from the galaxy's center. The spatial distribution of this outflow appears to be constrained by the galaxy's dense gas and dust disc. This discovery offers valuable insights into the early galaxy evolution, particularly in relation to powerful outflows in galaxy mass during the era of intense star formation.

The movement of fluid masses down slopes, influenced by gravity, forms turbulent plumes that are common in geophysical phenomena such as debris flows, landslides, avalanches, and sediment-laden river effluents. Entrainment of fluid into these plumes is critical to their growth and development, significantly impacting their final reach. However, the behavior of plumes with high fluid concentrations remains poorly understood. To gain insight into this phenomenon, we conducted a novel experimental study using particle image velocimetry to measure the vertical velocity defect within turbulent plumes containing a high concentration of particles in a tank. The energy balance derived from our velocity defect profiles enabled us to quantify the decay of turbulent kinetic energy and estimate the role of particle effects. The findings reveal that the maximum velocity defect decreases with increasing particle concentration, suggesting reduced exchange between the plume and surrounding fluid. The maximum velocity defect also decays exponentially with depth into the plume, influenced by particle concentration. The study's results are consistent with a maximum turbulence length scale that diminishes due to particle hindrance. Additionally, we developed a phenomenological model that accurately predicts the velocity defect in turbulent plumes, taking into account the effects of particles.

Understanding how epidemics spread over complex networks and their potential outcomes remains challenging due to theoretical limitations that prevent accurate prediction. In contrast, certain conditions under which extinction becomes virtually certain can be characterized mathematically using properties of random walks on graphs, specifically the principal eigenvalue. This study addresses a gap in these results by developing equivalent spectral criteria for hypergraphs, achieving extinction when the eigenvalue is positive, and conducting an in-depth analysis of the eigenvalue's behavior as it approaches zero.

Recent breakthroughs in magnetic 2D materials have revealed unique properties when they exhibit out-of-plane ferromagnetic order and strong spin-orbit coupling, resulting in robust spin-orbit textures even within a single layer. These characteristics allow for manipulating this order through electric fields and enable spin-texture control via coupling with external degrees of freedom, such as valley degree in 2D materials. The presence of valley degree of freedom also leads to valley polarization by such-ferrimagnetic order, leading to coupling between valley and spin degrees of freedom. In contrast to previous assumptions that require breaking spatial inversion or time-reversal symmetry, our findings demonstrate that Rashba-like terms arise from magnetic order and spin-orbit coupling, affecting the valley and spin textures. Our theoretical and density functional calculations reveal that Rashba terms impact both valley and spin degrees of freedom, thus providing a pathway for controlling valley and spin polarization through manipulation of magnetic order and providing a foundation for valley-based spintronics applications based on magnetic 2D materials.

Typical solar-like stars exhibit complex rotational patterns known as differential rotation, characterized by faster rotation rates at their poles compared to their equatorial regions. By incorporating realistic angular velocity distributions into mean-field solar-like dynamo models, we observe the impact of this rotation on the dynamics of magnetic cycles. These 3-D simulations reveal that stars with slower rotation rates exhibit weaker and later occurring magnetic cycles compared to those with quicker rotation rates. This outcome can be attributed to the presence of strong poloidal magnetic fields within these stars, which are essential for Dynamo theory, and are directly influenced by their rotational dynamics. Specifically, our models show that angular velocity distributions that favor the generation of strong poloidal magnetic fields tend to delay or even prevent the occurrence of cycles. Conversely, faster rotation rates facilitate the development of stronger toroidal magnetic fields, leading to stronger poloidal magnetic field generation through magnetic twist and shear effects, which in turn support cyclical dynamics.

Deep neural networks have achieved significant success in handling complex tasks like classification and regression by effectively addressing issues such as data labeling, dimensionality reduction, and feature extraction. This success has led to the exploration of complex input structures, such as graphs and multiple input channels, in neural networks. This research proposes a novel deep framework called Generalized K-fan Multimodal Deep Network (GKMDN) that efficiently processes various input types. Various configurations of GKMDN were tested and compared with state-of-the-art methods on tasks involving multiple inputs, such as classification with multiple channels and regression with conditions. The proposed framework demonstrated promising results and achieved significant improvements in handling complex input scenarios.

The use of multithreaded programs presents unique challenges in creating reliable software, primarily due to the presence of an enormous number of unpredictable thread executions characterized by varying timing. McMini, a model checker based on DPOR and implemented in Isabelle/HOL, helps identify essential, distinct threads that may contain design flaws resulting in unpredictable behavior. By being adaptable to various programming languages through a versatile framework supporting different memory models, McMini allows for efficient integration into design tools to provide thread traces highlighting potential risks in these heterogeneous programs.

Instant messaging has swiftly surpassed traditional news consumption channels, yet the spread of unverified information within these apps poses a significant problem. While messaging apps combat misinformation by monitoring and restricting notorious sources, another effective strategy involves curbing individual behavior. Research reveals that limiting the number of recipients who can receive a forwarded message can significantly reduce its propagation. A study of over 20,000 WhatsApp users who received a message promoting an undisclosed vaccine vaccine demonstrated that restricting each user from forwarding the message to a maximum of ten recipients led to approximately 30 recipients per user, whereas allowing each user to forward the message to ten contacts independently resulted in around 300 recipients per user. Notably, only the message's contents did not affect this behavior. These findings suggest that even minor structural modifications can substantially mitigate the spread of shared information.

We analyze a broad class of population models and derive an approximation for the distribution of allele frequencies at a specific locus. This approximation quantifies the probability that an allele drawn randomly from the population will originate from a particular lineage. The approximation is accurate to O(1/N), with errors stemming from rare events involving very small or very large family sizes, which decline exponentially as family size varies. To assess the approximation's effectiveness, our numerical results for a specific population model demonstrate that it accurately reflects reality even when the mean family size is close to unity, resulting in skewed frequency distributions.

Deep neural networks have made significant progress in spoof detection, but they face a common issue in spoofing countermeasure systems - the creation of sophisticated adaptations that are hard to detect and easily evade. To tackle this challenge, our approach moves away from fixed-length representations by adopting a method inspired by human decision-making. By using a sentence-like representation, we can analyze how neural networks arrive at their conclusions about spoofing and pinpoint the exact moments that lead to a specific judgment. Furthermore, we've developed an innovative Attentive Activation Mechanism (AM) to emphasize the parts of the representation most relevant to spoofing, boosting the system's capability to differentiate spoofed samples from genuine ones. Experimental results on the latest ACM MM datasets demonstrate our AM's effectiveness in lifting error rates in spoofing countermeasure systems that use hidden Markov models trained on convolutional neural networks and residual networks. Notably, we've seen improvements in error rates for both models - from 19.5% to 24.5% for the CNN-based model and from 16.5% to 18.5% for the residual network-based model.

We investigate Supersymmetric Effective Field Theories of inflation by modifying the Einstein scalar multiplet degree of freedom, initially proposed by Henneaux and Szabo, within a specific Effective Field Theory framework. By incorporating auxiliary fields and completing supersymmetry globally, then locally with supergravity in four dimensions, we explore the implications of this framework, particularly noting that certain supergravity limits cannot support de Sitter vacua with global supersymmetry. Furthermore, we examine the constraints imposed by global supersymmetry on higher-derivative corrections and discuss potential directions for future research.

Typically, the spatial symmetry of phase-space two-photon correlations matches the optical element being used, such as when a polarizing beam splitter results in four correlated pairs if four different wavelengths are used. Our research shows that in nonlinear crystals, there are inherent asymmetries in these correlations that don't match the optical setups. These hidden patterns can be revealed by post-selecting the results and are revealed to originate from the way the photons interact with the crystal at the atomic level. Our findings provide a clearer understanding of the connection between momentum and energy conservation in the process of spontaneous parametric down-conversion and reveal new ways to control phase-space quantum correlations.

Superconducting quantum circuits operating at microwave frequencies are emerging as leading platforms for quantum computing. Microwave radiation is commonly used to manipulate quantum states, while terahertz radiation in the near-field has the potential to offer unprecedented resolution for probing these modes. However, directly imaging terahertz near-field patterns at room temperature has been hindered by the limitations of traditional methods. A new approach using a copper tip and localized Joule heating enables direct observation of near-field terahertz patterns. This technique reveals the near-field distribution of superconducting resonators, uncovering previously inaccessible information about quantum coefficients and non-classical characteristics. Furthermore, it demonstrates the sensitivity and spatial resolution capabilities of this technique, paving the way for its application in studying higher-order quantum phenomena and transitions at terahertz and optical frequencies.

Given an arbitrary non-separable quotient $X/G$, where $X$ is the real line and $G$ is a group acting on $X$ with cardinality less than or equal to the cardinality of the real line, we demonstrate that $X$ can be divided into uncountably many null sets such that the quotient map maps these sets to uncountably many sets with large cardinality in the sense of Levy within $G$.

The rapid growth of investor numbers and available investment choices might be attributed, in part, to a shifting investment landscape beginning around 2007. This period coincides with the emergence of previously inaccessible investment opportunities following the subprime mortgage crisis. To better understand the dynamics at play, we employed agent-based models incorporating various investment strategies and observed that a considerable decline in equity, fixed income, and fixed income plus strategy performance could be explained by heightened competition from other investors. Our findings also reveal that newer investment approaches such as managed funds, dynamic asset allocation, and target date strategies initially boosted returns but eventually led to existing strategies seeing reduced returns due to the transfer of alpha returns. Our model outcomes indicate that while these newer investment strategies bring value to the market as a whole, they may not benefit every investor

Identifying network security threats from packet data stream has been a primary function of network monitoring tools since their inception. Despite being essential for detecting anomalies in network traffic, existing monitoring tools such as PcapPlusPlus, pyshark and libpcap exhibit vulnerabilities to manipulation due to their reliance on static, protocol number assignments rather than dynamic detection methods. If an attacker modifies the protocol number in a packet, traditional dynamic detection methods fail and the associated security monitoring capabilities degrade. To counter such assaults, a real-time dynamic protocol detection approach based on a modified maximum flow algorithm has been proposed for PcapPlusPlus, pyshark and libpcap. Furthermore, two manipulation strategies have been developed to simulate attacks on these network monitoring tools.

Developing complete circuitry that incorporates both superconducting and magnetic components allows the manipulation of magnetic quanta, known as magnons, through well-established quantum principles such as interference and entanglement. Our research demonstrates that close proximity to a superconductor effectively confines or contains magnons, showcasing an essential gate functionality necessary for the integration of magnetic and superconducting elements into quantum circuits. This phenomenon occurs due to the coupling between the magnetic/diffusive environment and the nearby superconductor's non-equilibrium state, which modifies the environment's self-energy and thus its response to magnons. This gate exhibits notable characteristics including symmetry with respect to the injected current direction and independence from the specific conduction mechanism whether through a tunnel barrier or metal. Additionally, the phenomenon exhibits sensitivity that depends on several variables such as the distance to the superconductor, its critical temperature, and temperature itself.

A prominent challenge in audio classification is overcoming data limitations, particularly when it comes to acquiring large, comprehensive, and diverse datasets. Such datasets are often costly and time-consuming to gather due to their complexity. Introducing new classes to existing datasets exacerbates this challenge by exacerbating data scarcity issues even further. Furthermore, collecting such data poses significant privacy concerns. The emergence of federated learning as a promising solution enables multiple data owners to collaborate in audio classification without sharing their data, effectively addressing both scalability and privacy concerns. Combining federated learning with novel classes in audio processing represents an even greater challenge, as existing frameworks are designed around the assumption of shared data labels. This paper introduces ZFLC, an innovative approach for performing zero-shot federated learning with new classes, and evaluates its efficacy on real-world audio datasets.

There have been various approaches to measuring Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states across different dimensions, yet a unified methodology encompassing all dimensions remains absent. We present a research paper with a detailed mathematical framework for the total measurement of comprehensive high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states across any dimension. Our methodology incorporates the principles of total measurement and symmetry, employing specifically designed multi-port interferometers constructed through the application of Clifford matrices. We successfully applied this method to experimentally verify comprehensive three-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states utilizing photonic entangments. Our design method can extend to scenarios involving any dimension, any dimensionality, and any number of particles, providing a dependable basis for experimental implementation and post-selection-free high-dimensional quantum communication protocols.

This research delves into the area of Reflecting Surface-Aided Mobile Communications by concentrating on the challenge of channel estimation in a MultiInputSingleOutput system that supports multiple users. A highly efficient and low-complexity solution is developed by designing a two-stage estimator, which leverages the inherent structure of the overall channel. The overall channel is composed of two components: the direct link between the base station and the user, and the indirect link via a reflectarray. Due to the simplicity of the overall channel, it can be represented as the product of two sparse vectors. Consequently, it is feasible to separately estimate each vector with significantly fewer pilot symbols compared to the total number of channels. Furthermore, the proposed estimator employs iterative refinement to enhance estimation accuracy. Moreover, two reflective strategy algorithms are presented: one that uses estimated channels to determine the optimal phase of the reflectarray, and another that accounts for the non-convex nature of the problem. A notable aspect of this work is the demonstration that the overall channel can be accurately estimated using a considerably smaller number of pilot symbols compared to the total number of channels. This is supported by theoretical analysis and confirmed through numerical simulations, which also showcase the performance benefits of the proposed estimator. Additionally, the reflective strategy algorithms yield performance comparable to optimal solutions.

This study provides insights into how U.S. local news online outlets addressed the COVID-19 pandemic between March 2020 and March 2021. Leveraging BigNews, a dataset of over 100 million headlines, we found that local news online significantly increased coverage of COVID-19 news and related topics. Our analysis also reveals that these outlets initially responded to the pandemic by reporting on a range of issues, but eventually shifted to reporting more consistently on COVID-19 cases and deaths. We observed correlations between local news online and pandemic metrics, such as cases and deaths, as well as socioeconomic factors, at different geographical scales. Our results show that this news was more closely correlated with these variables in larger and more populous areas. Our study also examined the relationship between local news online and media consumption patterns, as well as newspaper and newspaper online audiences, before and during the pandemic, and found that local news online has maintained its prominence in the news landscape, outperforming other media outlets.

This study investigates the feasibility of neural networks, specifically augmented with recurrency and enabled to learn from experience, to mimic basic cognitive functions found in the human brain responsible for understanding time and counting. We developed an architecture inspired by the biological brain and trained it to reproduce results from experimental studies on human counting progression across different age groups. The research reveals that this neural approach can replicate key characteristics of counting progression observed in both humans and animals, including the irregular distribution of counting skills across different age groups, the prevalent use of base-five counting systems, and the transition from additive to multiplicative counting methods. Notably, we found that artificial intelligence can reproduce patterns of counting progression that exhibit universal qualities across species and cultures, providing insights into these shared cognitive phenomena.

Bloom filters are widely employed for rapid, approximate set membership checks, utilizing bitmaps and hashing to determine if an element exists in a set, albeit with the drawback of requiring substantial storage space. In contrast, Bloom filter variants such as Bloom bitset filters and Xor filters mitigate this space complexity by exploiting element correlations to reduce the required storage bandwidth. Our space-efficient bitwise operations-based framework enhances the understanding and development of such filters, specifically showing that Xor filters outperform existing solutions in terms of effectiveness and efficiency while maintaining low memory requirements. Our analysis reveals that Xor filters are typically smaller and faster than traditional Bloom and Cuckoo filters, achieving up to 20% improvement in both aspects and allowing for a 2-4 times increase in capacity without compromising performance.

We establish a connection between convex functions and plurisubharmonic functions, revealing algebraic-analytic properties of global convex analysis. Furthermore, we derive analogues of fundamental concepts such as conjugate functions, subdifferentials, and h-concavity from Poincaré-Fenchel duality and complex analysis.

Traditional price-based models attempt to forecast the market's future direction, 
but our approach shifts focus to past price data, analyzing its effect on past 
market movements. We propose novel features based on past price patterns, 
associated with movement direction, duration, and volume. Our model leverages 
these features, paired with traditional features, within a gradient boosting 
algorithm. Testing on historical data revealed that future-price-based models 
show only marginal improvements over our novel approach, suggesting past market 
behavior contains valuable insights into future market movements. This finding 
also implies that traditional market efficiency may be somewhat limited.

This paper presents a privacy-preserving framework for federated learning (FL) that incorporates differential privacy and robustness against malicious participants. To counteract biases introduced by non-malicious users' noisy data updates, an advancedFedAVG aggregation method is utilized, incorporating an inverse variance weighting mechanism for FL. This is complemented by a novel FL approach called FLVoogd, which integrates differential privacy into the FL process, utilizing a Laplace distribution for noise injection into the server. The server then recovers a differentially private model by subtracting the injected noise, and applies a soft voting mechanism for label prediction. The performance of proposed FL methods is thoroughly evaluated using public benchmark datasets, and results demonstrate their effectiveness in ensuring privacy and detecting anomalies.

We introduce a new approach to bridge the gap between simulated and real images, specifically designed to transfer knowledge from one domain to another without mirroring the target domain. This tool enhances the effectiveness of source-based pre-training strategies by simulating real-world conditions, often seen in studies that utilize CARLA for autonomous driving applications in end-to-end tasks. Our method leverages the consistent structure of images, particularly prominent in end-to-end driving tasks that employ convolutional neural networks, to convert source-domain images to their target-domain counterparts without the need for domain-specific labeling. By pinpointing the most relevant layers in task-specific models that capture image semantics, we devise gradient projection techniques to project higher-layer domain-specific features onto lower domain-invariant features, effectively modifying the pre-trained task source images. These techniques exhibit improved results in both image transformation and transferability compared to existing methods, yielding notable gains of up to 15.5% in the case of vehicle detection. Furthermore, we showcase the utility of this method in developing end-to-end driving policies by refining the domain shift, resulting in performance gains of up to 15.5% in vehicle detection.

Significant progress in deepfake detection has led to the emergence of more sophisticated generation techniques that can create convincing manipulations. This progress poses a major threat to forensic media analysis, as current methods are primarily effective on clearly identifiable deepfakes. To address this challenge, our research aims to develop a novel deepfake generation framework that is both robust and transferable across a wide range of media content, and a corresponding detection method capable of identifying deepfakes on diverse content. To this end, we employ knowledge distillation in our framework to train a robust generator, and our detection method capitalizes on the discrepancies between the trained and real deepfake distributions. Additionally, we address the challenge of detecting deepfakes on content that was not part of the training set. Our approach and the dataset we developed, containing mid-level features for various types of media, are made publicly available to support further research in this field.

Identifying sub-Neptune exoplanets beyond their stellar hosts remains a formidable challenge, given the current capabilities of direct imaging, high-resolution spectroscopy, and photometric techniques. The detection of atmospheric oxygen in super-Neptunes like TRAPPIST-10d and TRAPPIST-1e has led researchers to propose the presence of water oceans supported by mineral reactions in their mantles, albeit with uncertain depths and internal pressures. The incorporation of these oceans into hydrostatic planets would leave imprints on their atmospheres and internal structures. Utilizing machine learning codes like tlite to simulate these internal structures and developing new spectroscopic methods, we show that the combined analysis of transit photometry and high-resolution atmospheric spectroscopy holds the potential to verify these proposed ocean models. The detection of an ozone absorption signature at around 11 $\mu$m would provide conclusive evidence for the presence of an ocean on these planets. The proposed approach relies on readily available data and techniques, and does not necessitate new technology.

Recent breakthroughs in developing artificial neural networks that mimic human-like intelligence have shown significant promise in creating automated systems capable of performing complex tasks. Neural networks inspired by the human brain, known as spiking neural networks (SNNs), demonstrate remarkable efficiency by using less power and taking less computation time, thanks to their ability to model temporal dynamics in sequences of events. Despite these advantages, previous research on SNNs has been limited to learning simple patterns in basic datasets, which don't reflect the simplicity and efficiency seen in nature. In contrast to recent studies that showcase improved performance using advanced algorithms, our work aims to demonstrate that basic spiking networks can learn patterns in sequence-based data effectively. Our results reveal that these basic networks achieve accuracy comparable to more complex networks with fewer parameters and can match or exceed their performance in time-critical applications, demonstrating their potential to create efficient artificial intelligence.

This document serves as the report for the Out-of-Category Research Challenge, which was established to explore novel research avenues outside the scope of Category-Specific. The report outlines the challenge's rationale, execution, and findings.

A new approach has been developed to measure the accuracy of Generalized Polynomial Chaos expansions (GPC) in approximating solutions to complex scientific and engineering problems with uncertain inputs. By utilizing the Generalized Finite Element Method (GFEM), which incorporates multiple length scales into solutions despite incorporating complexity such as cracks or interfaces, our approach enables the efficient analysis of highly sophisticated GPCH expansions. We present two novel a posteriori indicators that gauge solution accuracy without requiring prior knowledge of the problem's characteristic scale. Our approach also offers the advantage of determining the optimal generalization of Polynomial Chaos expansions for use in uncertainty-based analyses. Our method has been successfully applied to several challenging GFEM-based problems involving randomness, including those with cracks and multiple distinct length scales.

This research develops novel adaptive algorithms that utilize the generalized Bayesian information criterion (GBIC) for the online identification of sequential changes in systems with incomplete information. It achieves this through combining algorithms that detect changes and isolate them in fully observed systems. The detection algorithm periodically measures system data at a fixed interval, while the isolation algorithm continuously monitors specific system variables to pinpoint the time of each change and identifies its cause. The proposed GBIC-based identification algorithm integrates results from these two algorithms. It uses statistical thresholds to confirm the timing of each change, and relies on the algorithm's ability to accurately isolate changes to ensure precision in identifying them. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed identification method are supported by theoretical findings that demonstrate how isolation and detection work together to accurately identify changes. The accuracy of the GBIC algorithm in identifying changes is also assessed using simulations in realistic industrial settings, and the results show strong performance in systems with incomplete information.

The analysis of ancient stellar populations in dwarf galaxies reveals that they deviate from the simple model, revealing instead a complex population with varying ages, further exposing the limitations of relying solely on the metallicity distribution function for insights into galaxy formation. Furthermore, this research indicates that the majority of these galaxies underwent rapid transformation within the first 1-2 billion years, contradicting theories of gradual galaxy development. Instead, these findings support the theory that dwarf galaxies grew primarily through the accretion of smaller subunits, whose individual star creation and metal enrichment processes left a legacy in the form of diverse stellar populations. Ultimately, this complex population of ancient stars in dwarf galaxies reflects the diverse architectural plans of these ancient galaxies.

Given a continuous action of a profinite group $\Gamma$ on a commutative ring $R$, this work defines a homotopy fixed spectrum E_{\Gamma}M for any spectrum E and any R-module S. It then shows that homotopy fixed spectra obey certain universal properties and establishes connections between E_{\Gamma}M and traditional completed group cohomology when E and S have particularly nice properties.

A key challenge in building NLP models for document understanding is the high expense of obtaining labeled training data, which has led research groups to explore the use of large, publicly available datasets like DUDD to train models that can then be fine-tuned on smaller, client-specific datasets with limited labels. However, this approach risks causing a negative transfer in learning, hindering model performance on tasks requiring rich datasets and leading many groups to instead rely on heavily augmented data-labeling cycles. Our solution involves a new data augmentation technique that enhances data by leveraging worker expertise during both training and inference on rich NLP datasets, achieving near-parity with labeling costs. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on rich NLP extraction tasks and on paper title labeling, outperforming augmented data-labeling cycles with a improvement of 4-10% in F1 score on rich in-domain datasets and reducing labeling expenses by up to 70%.

The interface between EuS and ferromagnetic InAs in a EuS/InAs/Si structure exhibits unique properties that differ from bulk InAs due to the influence of the europium sulfide layer. The distinctive electronic structure at the interface, characterized by distinct bands, arises from the hybridization between the cation states of InAs and the sulfur atoms. In a specific linking configuration, where the atoms at the interface bond together, the energy of this hybridization is significantly higher than the bulk InAs energy due to strong covalent bonding. Conversely, in the non-linked configuration, the cation states exhibit a significant energy gap with the anion states due to the absence of hybridization. The effective magnetic field applied by the magnetized EuS layer to InAs at the interface is confirmed by the shift in spin polarization of the cation states.

We establish an optimal classification for Borel Wadge classes, refining Lippels classification, and prove that every Wadge class has either countably infinite or zero cardinality. This new classification simplifies and outperforms existing ones, having a lattice structure and explicitly identifying each Wadge class. Our method relies on introducing new operations on sets of reals and examining the resulting Wadge classes. The employed methods are general and may find application in other contexts.

High-precision deep learning model training requires significant computational resources and memory, posing challenges for large-scale deployments. To mitigate this issue, our research introduces ClickTrain, an innovative fine-grained architecture-preserving pruning algorithm that accelerates and enhances the scalability of deep learning training. ClickTrain preserves the original structure of neural networks while removing only redundant operations, resulting in minimal loss of model accuracy. The technique allows for automatic adaptation of network architectures based on hardware capabilities, optimizing the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The effectiveness of ClickTrain is demonstrated through experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation tasks, which show superior model accuracy and up to 4.1x speed improvements compared to existing deep learning acceleration methods. The clicktrain algorithm is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/clicktrain/clicktrain.

We investigate how to incorporate modal operators into linear logic semantics by expanding the Lambek Calculus with specific rules. These rules ensure that necessary and possibly operators have accurate and comprehensive interpretations in frames derived from complete lattices.

The merging of neutron stars with black holes produces gravitational waves, revealing secrets about these objects. Detecting these signals, however, remains difficult due to the vast number of potential waveforms. New approaches using neural networks in gravitational wave astronomy are making it easier to process data and classify detections quickly. Our research explores how different neural networks identify and classify GWNSBH signals, comparing their performance and efficiency. We examine the effects of waveform options, noise conditions, and detector variations on the networks' capabilities. The results show that certain configurations of neural networks can achieve high accuracy at identifying black hole masses, outperforming traditional methods while offering significant computational advantages.

A comprehensive study of exoplanet TOI-5542 has been conducted, incorporating novel findings from data obtained using various tools, including Gaia, the ground-based TESS, and the NASA/TESS telescopes. TOI-5542 is located approximately 220 light-years from the solar system and features a 0.79 solar mass star with the spectral type G5V, characterized by low metallicity and an older estimated age of around 7 billion years. TOI-5542 hosts a confirmed exoplanet, TOI-5542b, with a radius of 1.25 times that of Jupiter and a massive orbit spanning 677 days. Utilizing stellar data, the mass of TOI-5542b is estimated to be 1.15 times the mass of Jupiter, resulting in a surface gravity of 250 cm/s^2, which is typical of large, gas-dominated planets. TOI-5542b is classified as a subclass HA, or hot Jupiter, despite its current low equilibrium temperature of 210 K, likely due to the significant distance it traverses in its highly eccentric orbit with a 0.740 eccentricity. The discovery of TOI-5542 is notable for its unusual low metallicity, particularly in light of the generally accepted correlation between host star metallicity and the abundance of certain types

A constrained Markov decision process (CMDPC) has emerged as a valuable model for developing risk-sensitive and constraint-aware decision-making systems in operations research and control theory. We study a variant of the discounted, deterministic discount factor-driven CMDPC, characterized by its primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and optimality gaps. These quantities are efficiently computed via linear programming. We then formulate a mixed-integer linear programming problem to minimize the maximum primal-dual feasibility gaps, which our numerical results demonstrate can effectively reduce these gaps to near-zero, thus providing an efficient heuristic for approximating the CMDPC's optimal solution.

This research outlines a comprehensive methodology for recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions, emphasizing the significant knowledge these expressions convey. Mathematical expressions play a crucial role in accurately communicating scientific and technical information in written and spoken language, and understanding this message is essential for maintaining existing knowledge. Currently, offline recognition of mathematical expressions remains limited and hinders effective communication. By integrating existing methods, our proposed system achieves high-accuracy recognition of complex equations by addressing issues related to expression structure and character-level variability.

We investigate sheaf cohomology from the perspective of superquantum mechanics. In this context, the Euler characteristic of sheaves is interpreted as an index. It is demonstrated that the absolute values of these indices formed by line bundles on a projective variety P ultimately stabilize and obey periodic functions related to the cohomology dimensions of its tangent bundle. These findings for variety P can be further understood by applying Cline, Van den Bergh, and Cautis's work that links the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on P to a superquantum system with specific Hilbert spaces and operators. This category is known to be self-dual under this correspondence.

To examine the characteristics of variability in interaction processes within network systems, we initially employ a simple model representing a firefly synchronization mechanism to generate random networks with diverse topology variations. By analyzing these models using statistical tools such as the coefficient of variation and probability density functions, we identify and differentiate four distinct processes governing fluctuations in network dynamics, namely Poisson-based variation, exponential distribution, irregular irregularity, and underdispersion. Subsequent simulation of another network model allows us to correlate these variability processes with differences in network topology and further investigate their relationships with network size differences. Our findings contribute to a comprehensive understanding of network dynamics and have implications for the classification and interpretation of more complex system interactions.

Recently, many studies have employed Malevich method to improve policy learning in actor-critic reinforcement learning, resulting in faster convergence. However, the current implementation, which relies on linearization, results in lower sampling efficiency and policy accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce a new method that utilizes Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to perform more efficient exploration around the optimal policy. This new approach, while maintaining convergence rates, allows for a larger step size, leading to substantial improvements, as evidenced by up to a 20x faster exploration compared to Malevich. Additionally, we observe that our method results in better policy accuracy, as demonstrated by experimental evaluations on Gym environments.
By utilizing properties related to prime distribution, specifically von Ig's Lemma and Rosser and Schoenfeld's inequality, an elementary proof is conducted that supports the Twin Prime Conjecture.

Achieving precise and smooth vehicle movement poses a significant challenge in automated driving systems. The development of advanced navigation strategies such as sampled data control, predictive control, and their variations over multiple time steps has shown promising results but comes with notable drawbacks including processing delays, system complexity, real-time computation constraints, and the need for up-to-date state information. To overcome these limitations, a new approach called layered navigation was proposed. By combining lower-level sampled data control with higher-level multi-objective optimization, this strategy allows for seamless movement even when some state variables are unmeasured or difficult to access. However, this method's performance is significantly improved with the addition of sonar integration for better obstacle detection, integration that currently lacks in the literature but has been successfully implemented and tested here with an autonomous vehicle platform featuring sonar sensors arranged in a circular pattern. By incorporating sonar data into the navigation strategy, the system was able to achieve a substantial reduction in movement jerks during a challenging tracking task.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune, exhibits characteristics typical of outer solar system objects. Its surface composition is primarily constrained by measurements of its reflectance, although the Nereid's irregular shape poses challenges for accurate interpretation of data. Recent observations from the Nereid NII spacecraft have enabled the analysis of Nereid's surface features, revealing the complex ice mixtures present on Nereid's surface. By applying a two-component mixing model to Nereid's near-infrared spectral data, researchers have determined that Nereid's ice composition is consistent with that of water and CO2 ice. By incorporating shape constraints, researchers have estimated the CO2 ice proportion on Nereid's surface, finding it to be less than 10%. These results have implications for understanding the formation and evolution of Nereid, as well as its relationship with other trans-Neptunian objects.

We establish that specific lower triangular matrix groups give rise to distinct, non-isomorphic projective lines, which in turn determine the line geometries of specific affine and projective planes. These groups involve matrices of specific structures over a commutative ring with a nonzero nilpotent element. To prove non-isomorphism, we demonstrate that certain geometric configurations cannot be mapped to others while preservingincidence relationships in these planes and lines.

We examine specific models of set theory that demonstrate the impact of modifying certain powerful axioms on the definition of basic mathematical operations and the comparison of complex functions through changes in their values.

This study presents an innovative approach using negative drift and negativity in dynamic treatment regimes to enhance the efficiency of patient subgroups in Bayesian learning contexts. We begin by defining novel concepts negativity and minimum negativity along with associated optimization problems, providing both algorithmic solutions and performance bounds through algorithms named Bayesian Policy Optimization for Negative Drift (BPO-ND) and Bayesian Policy Optimization for Negative Drift with Minimum (BPO-NDM). Our analysis demonstrates that the excess risk incurred by BPO-ND is bounded within O(d^2 log(T)/epsilon^2 + d^2 epsilon^2/T + d^2 log(T)epsilon^2/T + d^2 log(2/epsilon)/epsilon^2), and the achievement times for BPO-NDM are estimated to be either O(d^2 log(T)/epsilon^2) or O(d^2 log(T)/epsilon^2 + d^2/epsilon^2 log(2/epsilon)), showcasing improved efficiency compared to previous Bayesian methods. The proposed approach has been validated through extensive simulations, showing its effectiveness in experimental data related to the ADHD treatment protocol developed by Kennedy et al.

This paper examines relationships between various categories associated with commutative algebras over a comonad, focusing on equivalences that connect them. A key focus lies in comparing two algebraic structures: those compatible with a comonad's smash product and those preserving its coproduct. We demonstrate equivalences between these structures for both commutative monads and comonads. Furthermore, these equivalences have significant applications to homological principles in comonadic transfer and monadic descent, effectively utilizing a dual version of Kuhn's theorem. As a result, certain comonadic transfer spectra turn out to be total derived functors.

A recent inquiry by Spekkens and Wallman (2020) (SW) (arXiv:1912.01752) proposed utilizing $E_8$'s core hole structure to model quantum physics, suggesting its relevance extends to all complex structures, not just integer-based ones. Following up on this, this research investigates whether the non-integer version of the $E_8$ core system can still explain quantum nonlocal phenomena like entanglement and contextuality without resorting to the real structure's shadow hole system. Contrary to expectations, it was found that using a rational-based echelon structure fails to accurately represent the required probability values for entanglement and contextuality, particularly the 1/4 and 1/8 values. Consequently, SW's result does not accurately reflect the ability of the complex $E_8$ core system to model quantum physics, although it remains valid for integer-based structures.

We investigate superconductivity in systems with many-body interactions where we employ a method that many-body perturbation theory can be applied in an systematic and controlled manner. Focusing on smooth, topologically protected bands within three-dimensional systems with strong spin-orbit coupling, our studies reveal that superconducting states with unconventional pairing symmetries are created via higher-order interactions. These states exhibit distinct characteristics including nodal lines, gapped surfaces, or fully insulating surfaces where topological protecting mechanisms are absent. Our results indicate that the emergence of these unconventional superconducting states can be determined by a specific order parameter that is based on the quantum spin Hall phase. Moreover, our studies also show that certain characteristics of the normal state, such as Fermi arc surfaces or chiral Kerr effect, can persist within the superconducting state due to the protection of time-reversal symmetry, even in the presence of interactions that break particle-hole symmetry.

Presence-absence data is commonly collected in ecological studies as binary records. Clustering has become a crucial analytical tool for processing this data in ecology. This study compares the performance of different data transformation and distance measurement techniques with various clustering methods on ecological datasets. To evaluate accuracy, the study employs established external validation metrics that relate sample groups to pre-defined species types. Two significant findings emerge: (1) data transformation methods have a substantial impact on subsequent cluster analysis and (2) there is no single approach that consistently yields accurate results across all ecologically motivated clustering tasks.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has seen significant advancements, yet novel architectures continue to be proposed at a rapid pace. While existing methods draw inspiration from various network designs, there has been a lack of comprehensive evaluation that clarifies the benefits and drawbacks of different architectures for salient object detection. This study introduces a unified framework to assess the performance efficiency of various salient object detection methods on both RGB and RGB-D images. The framework integrates six different salient object detection architectures, incorporating the novel DILSA method, and evaluates their performance using ten efficiency metrics. By integrating efficiency considerations, this unified framework sheds light on the trade-offs between different architectures and their underlying principles, ultimately guiding the development of more efficient deep neural networks for salient object detection.

The UM-IU@LING system for the SemEval-2019 task on detecting aggression in social media posts involved two models: one using Word2Vec and an SVM to classify tweets as aggressive or not, and another using BERT that could handle multiple classes including neutral content. The BERT model outperformed the SVM model on the test dataset.

This paper delves into the properties of integers that can be represented by both a binary string and its reverse (a palindrome) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine). We examine the characteristics of the integers formed by the quotient of the numbers derived from these two types of binary strings (non-palindrome quotient numbers, N-PQNs) and the ones formed by the quotient of the numbers derived from the binary string and its reverse (a palindrome) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine). We demonstrate the infinite existence of N-PQNs and integers formed by the quotient of the binary string and its reverse (a palindrome) as well as one that only has the binary string representation (a non-palestine). Moreover, the set of N-PQNs is shown to be closed under the operation of finding common divisors and the set of PQPs is shown to be closed under the operation of division by squares. Computed Tomography (CT) creates cross-sectional images using X-ray technology by measuring its energy-dependent polyenergetic properties. To enhance image quality and accuracy, a novel reconstruction method has been developed that combines matrix factorization and block coordinate descent algorithms. This method simultaneously addresses CT reconstruction, sensor denoising, and material decomposition through a non-convex variational approach. The resulting algorithm converges under specific conditions and demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques in polynomial time. The method has been successfully applied to joint reconstruction of polyenergetic CT data, achieving promising results in simulated data and real-world data from a dual-energy CT sensor with varying levels of noise.

Handwritten Text Recognition technology holds immense potential to improve accessibility for individuals with writing disabilities. However, their primary limitation lies in the scarcity of training data available. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel data enhancement technique that learns from observing how individuals with writing disabilities compose text cognitively and incorporates these insights into the training process. The approach enables models to predict missing text segments based on existing content and incorporates variability to reflect real-world scenarios. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that this Composition-based Data augmentation method yields significant improvements, particularly in instances with limited data availability.

Molecular dynamics simulations involving nuclei heavier than deuterium have proven to be a valuable tool in investigating the properties and reaction mechanisms of light nuclei. This research presents a breakthrough in the application of ab initio many-body theories to molten heavy nuclei beyond deuterium, specifically calcium-40. These calculations utilize a combination of quantum many-body perturbation theory and quantum Monte Carlo to model the nuclear interactions and incorporate atomic electron effects using ab initio methods. This work involved merging the atomic electron calculations with the nuclear simulations using quantum molecular dynamics. To model the interatomic forces, we employed the embedded atom method and utilized the eAMoRc method to correct the spurious charge leakage artifacts resulting from the use of Gaussian-type basis sets. Our initial calculations involved the compression of solid calcium and demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in reproducing experimental values for the interatomic force constants and chemical bonding. These calculations involved evaluating the total energy and analyzing the radial distribution functions of calcium-40 clusters consisting of eight or sixteen nuclei. These calculations utilized a fully merged approach that combined quantum Monte Carlo and time-dependent quantum many-body perturbation theory to correct the spurious charge leakage artifacts resulting from the use of Gaussian-type basis sets. These calculations exhibited strong agreement with experimental values of the interatomic force constants and demonstrated the efficacy of our approach in investigating the properties and reaction mechanisms of light nuclei.

One-dimensional systems exhibit distinct characteristics that set them apart from their two and three-dimensional counterparts, primarily manifested through phenomena such as edge states and Su-Schrieffer-Heeger topological insulators. These features can be understood through basic concepts of wave nature and particle behavior. Unlike conventional materials, topological insulators possess unique properties stemming from their concept of band structure. While these phenomena primarily concern electric charges, they also arise in various other contexts, such as observations made under extraordinary conditions or through direct analogies. To facilitate the mathematical description and experimental verification of these phenomena, researchers often turn to the SSH model. This model's simplicity makes it an excellent teaching tool for universities, where it can be effectively implemented in experiments using diverse methods.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain convex domains in several dimensions. Specifically, it characterizes the compactness of these operators across the Bergman spaces of convex regions at different degrees in multi-variable functions, as well as unit balls in functions containing a constant term, in dimensions three or higher. Additionally, the study establishes a comprehensive classification of compactness for this operator in the unit ball space in three dimensions.

We utilize the two-loop UV finiteness of N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory on a 5D anti-de Sitter space boundary to verify corrections to the tree-level AdS radius in four-dimensional supergravity theories originating from type IIB string theory. By employing a 5D boundary dual theory, we confirm the absence of renormalization of the AdS radius, thereby demonstrating a deeper connection between the four-dimensional boundary dual theory and the 5D anti-de Sitter space boundary dual theory, originally proposed in [arXiv:1312.7232]. Furthermore, we clarify the boundary condition of the 5D dual theory, where a specific boundary condition leads to the recovery of the four-dimensional supergravity theory, and we verify its loop stability, thereby strengthening the evidence of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

High-performance computing on CPU-GPU systems often suffers from limited expression capabilities due to CPU's word-oriented data handling and CPU-GPU memory unification. Most existing GPU memory allocators are tailored for array data, leaving a significant gap in supporting object-oriented programming. To address this limitation, we introduce DynaSOAr, a dynamic hash table-based memory allocator specifically designed to support object-oriented programming on GPUs in an high-performance manner. DynaSOAr enables efficient object memory allocation and collection, supports object resizing and data migration between CPU and GPU, and facilitates large-scale object management. Through fully parallel methods, DynaSOAr achieves superior performance compared to traditional GPU memory allocators and outperforms a custom-written GPU memory allocator. The integration of DynaSOAr within the OpenCL language allows users to program objects, and our prototype implementation demonstrates the feasibility of this approach. Theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm that DynaSOAr delivers enhanced efficiency and makes object-oriented programming a viable option for GPU-based applications demanding high performance, thus addressing performance degradation and limited expressiveness issues.

Standard models with a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry can be conceptualized as a
linear combination of chiral $U(1)$ symmetries stemming from either $E_6$ or
$SO(10)$ GUT models.  By examining all such models incorporating $U(1)_X$ as
a linear blend of $SO(10)$ generators, we identified 25 distinct models with
three, four, or five right-handed neutrinos, classified according to their
low-energy phenomenological characteristics and high-energy completion within
the $SO(10)$ framework.  Focusing particularly on the three-neutrino model
sector, we analyzed low-energy observable properties such as the relationship
between the $Z$ boson's coupling and lepton-flavor non-universality between
first and third generations, as well as the magnitude of the muon's anomalous
magnetic moment deviation from the standard model, which can be experimentally
observed.  We then assessed high-energy realizations within the $SO(10)$
framework, concentrating on the existence of specific field contents in the
126-dimensional Higgs field representation and their implications for
neutrino masses through see-saw mechanisms, thus informing model selection for
upcoming experimental validation.

Understanding the cane turtle's shell mechanics is essential in cane research. Computational models have shown that the pressurized cane tube's stress patterns align with the cane's curved shape, suggesting its potential use as a shield. A new experimental approach was developed to measure internal pressure effects on cane tubes by applying loads both longitudinally and circumferentially. The pressurized tubes exhibited reduced mechanical stiffness compared to unpressurized ones, with the pressurization causing significant changes in stress patterns by reducing longitudinal tension and introducing compressive forces. The findings highlight the importance of pressurization in the cane's mechanical stability.

In many situations, we can ensure a certain level of reliability in assessments by using Bayesian reasoning under uncertainty. By ensuring that our confidence intervals remain within specific limits, even in the face of uncertain model parameters, we achieve what is known as robustness assurance. This concept has significant implications, particularly when dealing with systems that have safety risks. Recent research attempts to tackle this problem by formulating it as an integer programming problem. However, this approach is limited to simple Bayesian networks and struggles with larger, more complex systems. To overcome these restrictions, we broaden the scope to include general credal networks and propose converting the problem into a search for the most optimal structure of a probabilistic circuit. By doing so, we develop an efficient method for assessing robustness in large-scale systems and present a practical solution using constraint relaxation. This approach ensures that our findings remain within a predetermined accuracy limit.

Researchers achieved B. Bloch oscillations using a one-dimensional phononic crystal made of alternating steel and aluminum segments. By adjusting the ultrasonic driving frequency within a specific range, they induced Bloch oscillations, which led to oscillating reflectivity that matched theoretical predictions.

A vector code is considered neighbor-transitive if the set of neighbors of any codeword only includes that codeword itself and its neighbors. This concept of neighbor-transitivity has proven particularly useful in the study of generalised quadrangles. In this article, we will explore neighbor-transitive codes within the framework of generalised quadrangles of types $C_n(q)$ and $D_n(q)$. Specifically, type $C_n(q)$ will yield three distinct partial spreads, while type $D_n(q)$ will yield three distinct partial spreads as well, all involving codes with high minimum weights. These findings provide novel examples of high minimum weight partial spreads in generalised quadrangles of types $D_n(q)$ and new lowest degree partial spreads with distance parameters $2q+2$ in the quadrangles derived from Ovoids and Tangents.

To quantify a self-similar anisotropic density framework proposed by Ostriker et al. for dense molecular rings like the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone, we employed 2D correlation functions to analyze a comprehensive set of radio and infrared tracers. Applying this methodology allowed us to precisely assess two key variables, $\gamma$ and $\eta$, that characterize an anisotropic Eulidian density framework by modifying the anisotropic Omkar normalization.
